subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF OFF-RESERVE PROGRAM TO ASSIST INDIANS

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF OFF-RESERVE PROGRAM TO ASSIST INDIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in keeping with government policy to provide the Indian people with the greatest opportunity to choose their own way of life, provision has now been made to extend housing assistance to Indians who wish to live away from reserve communities.
Effective today, employed Indian people can obtain assistance under the off-reserve housing program which will enable them to live closer to their work, to broaden their opportunities for continued employment and to live in the community of their choice. It will assist them to take advantage of the home ownership finance facilities which Canadians generally have available to them.
Under this program the Indian Affairs branch will provide a conditional grant up to a maximum of $6,000 for a house and $1,000 for furnishings. The amount available to each Indian will relate to his income and his ability to meet mortgage payments on the cost of the home over and above the conditional grant.
An arrangement has been made with my colleagues the Minister of Veterans Affairs and the Minister of Labour responsible for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, to assist in carrying out this program. The Department of Veterans Affairs will supervise the program. Their role will be to assist the Indian in his selection of a home suitable to his needs, and they will make certain that each home, either constructed or purchased conforms to the standards of the National Housing Act. Central mortgage and housing will be responsible for providing the mortgage funds required to cover the costs involved above the amount of the conditional grant.
The conditional grant will be secured by a second mortgage which will be forgiven if the applicant lives in the house for a ten year period. As hon. members know, Indians who live in reserve communities are now given
grants up to $7,000 for houses built on the reserves. It is one of the purposes of this program to ensure that there are not only no obstacles in the way of Indians who wish to live away from reserves, but that there are no financial disadvantages. It is the government's policy to encourage the Indian people to choose their own role in the Canadian community, just as every other Canadian does. This program will assist in meeting this objective.

An initial amount of one million dollars has been provided by my department to initiate the program.

Mr. Speaker, this announcement has been anticipated with a great deal of interest, particularly by the members of the Indian communities across Canada and also by all the members of this house. I am sure I can say that, because in recent months and years there has been a growing interest in the welfare of those to whom we like to refer as our first Canadians. When the minister announced the housing program for Indians on reservations last year it was felt it would have a negative effect unless some provision was made to meet the even more critical housing demand among our Indian citizens, that is accommodation for the Indians moving off the reservations.
The policies which have been established in recent years for our Indian citizens, the improvements in educational opportunities, the job counselling service which has been set up within the framework of the old unemployment insurance commission and now the National Employment Service, and of course the extension of the vote to our Indian population, all have had the beneficial effect of encouraging Indians to move into the general economy of Canada.
I know that one of the recommendations which recently came out of the committee, whose members have been active in examining the growing problems' of our Indian citizens, was that provision be made along the lines which have been announced here this morning. It was my privilege a few weeks ago to attend the conference on Indian affairs in Winnipeg which is sponsored every year by

Assistance to Off-Reserve Indians the greater welfare council of Winnipeg. This year it was handled entirely by the Indians themselves, and housing was one of the main problems discussed during that conference.
We hope the benefits of the program will become available immediately. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in making a few comments on the speech from the throne I should like to refer directly to the document itself and to some of the plus factors, you might say, and many of the minus factors which are evident in the speech.
On hearing the speech from the throne I believe the first thing which came to one's mind was the fact that this government is unsure of itself. We find in the speech that the government wishes to have a great deal of room to manoeuvre. Then sadly we notice that the only conclusion to which we can come is that the government's priorities are not necessarily the nation's priorities. At page 2 of Hansard we find this in the throne speech:
It is also conscious-
That is the government.
-that the advantages and disadvantages of the present constitutional structure are deeply intertwined.
Then it goes on:
Studies to obtain the best advice on this important matter are now under way with a view to subsequent consideration of the whole problem by parliament.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, it is an accepted fact that the reform of Canada's constitution is something that demands immediate and open discussion. It is now nearly three years since
May 16, 1967

the party I represent proposed a national conference on confederation. In those three years numerous studies have been made, numerous books have been written and numerous speeches have been made. Surely no one will deny that this subject is one which requires a thoughtful, reasoned and even cautious approach. But neither can it be denied that there never has been a time more opportune or a moment more significant than this centennial year to bring into the open the question of reform of the constitution of our country.
It is all very well to say that the study is going on. But why has this study taken place in darkened rooms with the doors closed and shutters drawn, with not even a flicker of a candle flame to cast a little light on the goings on? Why can it not be brought into the open in an open forum of discussion and opinion? Are we not a country which is mature enough to sit down and reason what our course must be?
I do not think there is any doubt that we are such a country. No one asks that this discussion be concluded overnight. We ask only that the people who love this country be given the opportunity, whether they be scholars or anything else, to express the spirit of their nationhood on the 100th anniversary of this country. After all, a constitution is more than a set of laws; it is the embodiment of a nation's conscience.
I do not suggest for a moment that the government should cease the studies it has undertaken. Rather I suggest that men with piles of books in these darkened rooms cannot capture this conscience for our nation. Let us cast aside every partisan consideration on the part of this government and convene this great constitutional conference. We cannot harm ourselves, and surely we can aid our progress through this second century. Let us have debate and discussion from one coast to the other coast. Let us instil in our people a sense of pride, and future pride, in their country, a pride proceeding from their full participation in deciding the destiny of our country. I think we should write an exciting prologue to parliament's consideration of our constitution. Let us do it now, to have in our remembrance of the centennial year this vital contribution to our future.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
Farther along on page 2 of Hansard of May 8, the speech from the throne goes on to read:
Today the main struggle is against social injustice, against cultural mediocrity, against spiritual stagnation and against all forms of intolerance.
The Address-Mr. Brand
These are fine words indeed. Let us take social injustice first. Where in this document is there an indication of one piece of legislation to ease social injustice? Where is the promised war on poverty? Where is there concern about the disabled and the sick? Where is there concern about mental illness, the greatest single cause of illness in our country? Yet the division of mental health in the Department of National Health and Welfare has been repositioned to a lower level. Apparently it is not considered important enough to be given the type of attention that it should be given. Does the government think its job is done in this field, or does it think that the setting up of another bank or network of computers will solve it? Does the government care? I am sure the people wonder if it does.
The throne speech mentions cultural mediocrity. Who are the government accusing of cultural mediocrity? Is it Expo '67 perhaps, or our musicians, our writers, our artists and our poets? Is it accusing Maureen Forrester, Leopold Simoneau, Glenn Gould or Wilfrid Pelletier? Does it accuse Donald Lautrec, Gordon Lightfoot, Harold Town, Hugh Mac-Lennan, the Royal Winnipeg Ballet or Les Feux Folets? Are those the people and the groups whom the government is accusing of cultural mediocrity? Someone says it did not accuse anyone. Perhaps this is a self accusation, because I think in Canada we have a very proud culture. I am quite sure that the people who are best known in this country are not the members of the government opposite but people like L. M. Montgomery, who wrote Anne of Green Gables in Prince Edward Island and Pauline Johnson in British Columbia. These names are well known in Canada, but how many know the Prime Minister? We know about the Group of Seven and W. O. Mitchell, but how many know the members of the government? I think it is indeed a strange thing to accuse anyone in this country of cultural mediocrity. This government seems to be blind to the enthusiasm, the excitement and the energy we have in our country.
The speech from the throne speaks about all forms of intolerance. I cannot agree more that we must fight against all forms of intolerance, but for whom is the government fighting? Is it fighting for our Indians and Eskimos? Perhaps the government have not yet seen the Indian pavilion at Expo. If they did they would see how the Indians speak with great eloquence in this pavilion. What indeed has the government done for these
May 16, 1967

The Address-Mr. Brand native peoples? We hear promises and platitudes; today we are told we will build a few more homes for the Indians off the reserves and this at a time when the Indians themselves are pointing out that not sufficient is being done on the reserves. It appears that this government is blind to the needs of the people of Canada.
Then there is mention of spiritual stagnation. The speech from the throne has certainly covered the field. Who is the government accusing of spiritual stagnation? Is it accusing itself again? Is it accusing the men and women of this country who seek a new kind of Christianity? Is it accusing people such as the author of The Comfortable Pew and the people who have been debating it ever since? Is it accusing those who are responsible for the Christian pavilion at Expo? Is the government accusing our late revered Governor General Vanier of spiritual stagnation, or perhaps Cardinal Leger? Does the government know whereof it speaks? Surely it is the government which increases bureaucracy that can be accused of mediocrity and stagnation. Let us not accuse the people of Canada just because the government has no faith in them. The people all across this nation are waking up. They are not going to stand much longer for this type of nonsense.
On page 2 of the throne speech we find the following statement:
The government will also take special measures in particular designated areas where human resources are not adequately utilized.
How long have we waited for this? How long has the government diddled and dawdled around letting the blind lead the blind before action is taken? The government goes on to say that it will take further measures for the retraining of adults, yet it seems to me that a few weeks ago in this house they were hurrying a bill through which had to do with the occupational retraining of adults. What was the matter with that bill? Did the government forget something? Is it adding something to it even before the legislation has had an opportunity to be carried out properly? This government is very strange; one end does not seem to know what the other end is doing. In the last few days we have had ample evidence of this strange polarity in the cabinet.
The throne speech refers to the involvement of the government in many matters; and so it should, because this government more than any other has continued the process of involvement and control. It takes money away and then gives it back with strings attached. Last year alone 11,000 new


civil servants were hired by the government, making a total of nearly 250,000 in the public and related services. A short while ago I read somewhere that under this present administration bureaucracy has increased by almost a third. When this government is unable to act and unable to take initiative it puts another group on the top and pays its salaries. It answers problems with more bureaucracy.
I am sure the hearts of the members of this house go out to the people of Canada who, petted, pampered and paid for from cradle to grave, are being protected from evil, shielded from thought, muzzled from expression by this government which admits in the speech from the throne that it is becoming increasingly involved.
No one wishes that there be people without food and shelter, without medical assistance or without the opportunity for advancement. In its half hearted attempt to protect the people of this nation the government has ordained that its task must be to stamp out spiritual stagnation and cultural mediocrity. It says to the people that it will take care of them, that it will raise their culture and spirit with bureaucracy and increased taxes. What a way to raise one's spirit. Thank God I have more faith in the people of this country than has this government. I am sure members on this side of the house would never be caught losing faith in the people who sent them here.
Undoubtedly there are some areas in this speech which are open to approbation. Even in a hash of analogies there is bound to be some truth. However, I will not go into them today. Many apologists from the other side will have already done this. I am sure their words are accurate in this regard, but I would rather spend a few minutes on what is lacking in the throne speech.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
Somewhere in this throne speech, Mr. Speaker, amidst all these platitudes and hyperbolic overtures there is a program. Most of it is old, weather beaten and a little cracked here and there. Some of it reflects the fact that the government cannot make up its mind whether or not to be Canadian. Part of this program, if it were only more specific, could help the country, although the government appears to want to help this country for the wrong reasons. However, as I pointed out before, the priorities are reversed. There are problems and questions facing this country that require solution. Some of these the government says it will face, but some are not even mentioned.
May 16, 1967

Where, for example, is legislation for the control of air pollution? Where is there any mention of action on the recommendations of the committee on drug costs and prices? We spent a long time in that committee, had many meetings and made many recommendations in a lengthy and reasoned report. Where in the speech from the throne is there any mention of an attempt by this government to do something about the cost of drugs in this country? I have the report here, Mr. Speaker, and I should like to refer to page 51:
Your committee has therefore come to the following conclusions:
1.	That the price of drugs in Canada is at least higher than it need be:
2.	That no significant change has taken place in the drug cost structure since the recommendations of the Hall commission which were primarily based on the recommendations of the restrictive trade practices commission;
I will skip a few recommendations, and then I find this:
7.	That the Implementation of the recommendations could alter in some respects the form of the drug industry as it exists today, removing inefficiencies in the industry and increasing competition;
8.	That in anticipation of national and provincial welfare programs or the further development of other forms of health services, it is of paramount importance that legislation be introduced at the earliest practical date to implement the recommendations of this committee.
I will repeat that:
-it is of paramount importance that legislation be introduced at the earliest practical date to implement the recommendations of this committee.
I could say a great deal about this problem. I have marked certain portions of the summary of recommendations contained in this report. Action could be taken by this government this session to lower the cost of drugs to the consumer. What has the government done? It has not even appointed a minister, though that is usually what they do, appoint another minister. I shall read recommendation No. 2:
That the personnel and facilities of the food and drug directorate be expanded to make possible the implementation of the recommendations of the Boyd committee, the Hilliard committee and this committee.
I shall not read all the recommendations, but I should like to refer hon. members to recommendations Nos. 2, 4, 5, 6, 9, 13, 17, 18, 20 and 21. All these recommendations clearly show what this government could do to bring forward legislation to amend various acts and introduce other measures to help the food and drug directorate bring down the cost of drugs 27053-17
The Address-Mr. Brand to the consumer. I should like to read recommendation No. 13:
That the federal sales tax be removed from the sale of prescription drugs.
I remind hon. members that instead of removing the tax this government has raised it from 11 per cent to 12 per cent. Instead of helping the people who need help, the old folk with large drug bills, what have they done? They have added another 1 per cent to the tax, which in reality amounts to about a 9 per cent increase in the tax itself. This is what this government has done to help the people of Canada. It is no wonder we feel that government has its priorities backward.
Where is legislation to protect our dairy farmers from bankruptcy? Where is legislation to guard against inflation and stop the spiralling cost of living? Make no mistake, Mr. Speaker, there are two things that are bothering the people of Canada today. The first is the increase in taxation and the second is the ever increasing cost of living. These are the two problems which are becoming an increasing burden to every Canadian. If something is not done about them soon I would not be the least bit surprised to see more than the farmers marching on parliament hill. I think it is about time some of the people who are going to visit Expo stopped at this place on their way to express some of their views on taxation and the cost of living.
There are many other matters with which I should like to deal, but time is of the essence in this debate. I should have liked to discuss parliamentary rules and procedures. Perhaps at some other time I can do so. I should have liked to go into this question in detail because it seems to me this government, although it is suggesting changes, once again has its priorities backward. I believe the government is suggesting changes in the wrong way. I just say that I do not agree with the priorities suggested.
It is not merely an allocation of time, not merely the shortening of debate or the rushing through of legislation that we need. What we need is an expanded opportunity to study legislation, to understand the implications of the legislation brought before the house. I believe we require a further change in the committee system, perhaps allowing the committees more freedom to frame legislation. Members should be given assistance beyond that rendered by the parliamentary library, the type of assistance which is so necessary to make a member a good parliamentarian. I must say I was very pleased to hear the

May 16, 1967
The Address-Mr. Brand Canadian Federation of Agriculture suggest today that research assistance be provided for members.
I mentioned earlier, Mr. Speaker, that no legislation had been announced to protect our dairy farmers from bankruptcy. In this connection I should like to refer to two articles in Farm and Country, the first of which is dated March 28, 1967 and headed "Ontario Industrial Farmers Must Have $5 Milk". This article is by Charles Munro, president of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture. Let me just read one paragraph:
The demand for $5 per hundredweight for milk used for industrial purposes is neither frivolous, greedy or unreasonable. As a recent resolution of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture says, even this price is still short of economic equality for producers.
This should not surprise anybody.
The second article which appeared in the same paper is dated April 11, 1967 and was written by the same gentleman:
Government policy is supposed to help the people, not drive them up the financial wall.
This is a thoroughly bad, thoroughly unacceptable policy. Mr. Greene was able-
I presume the writer is referring to our disabled minister or whatever he should be called:
Mr. Greene was able last summer to divert the wrath of dairy farmers toward Queen's Park and Quebec city, thanks to the unsophistication of those heading the protest movement. If he hopes this year to continue avoiding criticism by putting up another false front in the form of the Canadian Dairy Commission he is wrong. Farmers now have a little less Greene in their eyes than they did.
This seems to say a mouthful, as we used to say out west. I am not going to go into all the reasons this dairy policy is not acceptable. I believe the parliamentary secretary to the Secretary of State put the case very well yesterday, and I refer to what he said at page 230 of Hansard. This is one statement which I believe is rather good, if I can find it:
I would agree that such an argument might be true, but for an area such as Bonaventure and other less advanced areas where the number of dairy producers is less than a thousand with about 40 per cent having to look elsewhere for a supplementary income, those claims are fair and legitimate.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
That is a member of the government, a parliamentary secretary, speaking. I could not agree more. In view of this, Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Moore):
This house regrets that Her Majesty's advisers have failed to submit a program to give the dairy

farmers of Canada a guaranteed return on their product of $5.10 per hundredweight for all manufacturing milk.
With that in mind, Mr. Speaker, I wish in closing to say a few things about the speech from the throne. This speech makes pretty statements about confederation, but it ignores the meat of the matter. It ignores the fact of this nation and the strength of the nation. The strength of this or any other nation is in the strength of the individual and the collective strength of its peoples. Aside from these pretty statements, this government would have us even in this special year ignore the people. It would have us ignore their strength. It would even have us ignore their patriotism.
This is the government, Mr. Speaker, that takes away from our nation the heritage of our first one hundred years. This is the government that sneers at royalty, that would denigrate the fact that we are a constitutional monarchy, an example of the most stable form of government the world has ever seen. It is the same government that gives its people not leadership, not spirit or enthusiasm or even faith, but gives them commissions, studies, white papers, officials and ministers.
As we begin our second century as a nation, Mr. Speaker, let us recognize the needs of this great country. Let us recognize that there are two languages and two cultures. Let us allow our people to know one another, to understand one another. Let us give to our people no matter what language they speak the leadership they need in the cause of this unique country. In this centennial year let us rededicate ourselves as Canadians and as members of parliament to the principle that we are, above all, the representatives of the people who sent us here. Let us join with members of all parties to make this house more effective, with new rules, with television, if you want, with whatever is necessary. And let us never forget that this is the forum of the people; to use an old phrase, it is the wellspring of democracy.
We must protect and guide the interests of those we represent. We must encourage those who report our doings to them to be as objective and as factual as possible. But above all, Mr. Speaker, we must remember that if we are to have a new, proud Canada we must work to the limit of our abilities as individuals to preserve the freedom of purpose and choice that our people must have.
May 16, 1967

I conclude with one final quote from a former political science student at McGill University, Gerald Haslam; it is a very good one and I want to put it on the record:
Let us go forth together, and work as we must. Let us hold high our heads and be proud. Let us make of this nation of ours, greatness.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I should like to extend congratulations to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Like other hon. members who have spoken I too was impressed with the style and the manner in which both the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Jamieson) and the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Cote) carried out their duty.
Although I do not mean this in any unkind personal way I must say that I was left greatly confused, particularly by the subject matter of the speech of the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska. He would have us believe that the farmers of this country are quite satisfied with the current state of their industry and with the current price levels prevailing in agriculture. As has been said by the last speaker who just moved an amendment, this is certainly far from the case.
One reads in the throne speech paragraph after paragraph about the legislative intent of the government for the year 1967. A first reading of the speech would lead one to believe that this government has a lengthy list of legislative items with which it is very anxious to proceed in this special year. However, Mr. Speaker, it is the fact-I believe this has already been said-that of the entire throne speech only four items are new or original in this session. The others are items which have been carried over either from the preceding year or from the year before that. As my leader said on a previous occasion, this speech from the throne is a potpourri of leftovers.
I, like others here, should like to take the exhortation of the Prime Minister to heart, and would like to avoid making critical comment about this government's activities and the state of the nation. This after all is a special year, and the Prime Minister is no doubt right when he says we should not tear our hair as frequently as we have in past 27053-171
The Address-Mr. Schreyer years but should do a little more tub thumping. Yet surely it is not unreasonable, Mr. Speaker, to suggest and suggest strongly that there are hard pressing problems in the country today, and that because they are hard pressing we must engage in hard hitting debate. We must engage in a thoroughgoing analysis of these problems.
It does not take any precision in research to determine what are some of these hard pressing problems. They affect certain income groups and certain occupational groups with particular severity. The first hard pressing problem-and I use every word with deliberate intent-which exists in 1967 and which has existed for a decade or more is that having to do with the level of income being received by the food producers of this country. The hon. member for Saskatoon has just moved an amendment that is sharply critical of this government for its indecision, its procrastination and apparent intention to do nothing to adjust its milk policy so as to enable those who are engaged in milk production to remain in it and continue producing this necessary and vital commodity, not just in the short run but to make their income prospects and therefore production prospects viable and healthy in the long run. That is not being done, and that is why the amendment was moved. I hope that independent minded members on the other side will join this party in supporting that amendment.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
In recent weeks there have been new developments in agriculture. The Minister of Trade and Commerce told us something of the new wheat agreement which has been arrived at during the Kennedy round talks, and we gather from the minister's statement that the range of wheat prices under the new agreement will be increased by about 21 cents per bushel. That should be cause for neither joy nor gloom, and the government's optimism should be taken with a grain of salt. An increase of 21 cents means a 10 per cent increase, but in the last three or four years farm machinery has increased by more than 10 per cent, as anybody who has bought a combine in 1964, 1965 or 1966 is aware. A 12 foot self-propelled unit which then cost $9,000 now costs $12,000 to $14,000. The new unit may have a greater work capacity, but that is not enough to justify that degree of price increase. To be realistic, the new agreement does not cover the price increases of the last few years, so we farmers are in the same relative cost-price position we occupied in
May 16, 1967

The Address-Mr. Schreyer 1964. The president of the Manitoba's Farmers Union said to the press yesterday that a 40 cent to 50 cent per bushel increase was needed to ease the lot of the farmers he represents.
Farmers have been dissatisfied generally with this government's agricultural policies. When the Minister of Agriculture announced the new diary policy about a month and a half ago he tried to leave the impression that there would be substantially increased federal assistance, but had no satisfactory answer to the point that I raised, that the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Moore) repeatedly raised and that other hon. members raised, which was that it was illogical to draw artificial distinctions between surplus fluid milk and manufacturing milk. The minister says fluid milk comes under provincial jurisdiction, and that the federal government therefore ought not to be involved with support payments on fluid surplus milk. The fact is that all surplus fluid milk can be regarded as manufacturing milk and, taking the minister's own words, support for the price of manufacturing milk is a federal responsibility.
The new policy, resting on the foundation of artificial distinctions, does not help dairy farmers but aggravates problems which have grown more serious during the past several years. The Minister of Agriculture, in some of his actions and attitudes, reminds me of a jackass in a rainstorm. The jackass turns his back on the storm, hunkers up his back and takes it without doing anything about it. When the Minister of Agriculture is faced with the legitimate and organized storm of complaints of dairy farmers and spokesmen for the agricultural industry, he stands in one spot, hunkers up and refuses to say whether he will reconsider his policies. In the past I have accused the minister of revealing an attitude of indolent nonchalance toward agriculture, and I repeat that description today. The attitude of the government on agricultural commodity prices is one of indolence and nonchalance. That attitude is evident in other fields also.
Because the government, according to the throne speech, will appoint a special task force to look into agricultural problems we are to infer that we may rest easy. Yet clearly, that task force is an indication that this government has no farm policy it may call its own. There is nothing wrong with the federal and provincial ministers of agriculture and federal and provincial departmental officials meeting and formulating policy at some sort


of national farm policy conference. Spokesmen for the farmers unions and the federations have been urging for the last year or two that this be done, yet the minister has not said whether he will accommodate them. The task force mentioned in the throne speech may mean a royal commission, a special ad hoc interdepartmental committee of the federal government, or a similar committee composed of personnel from provincial and federal departments. Nobody knows. In the meantime we may be sure the government will use the task force as a pretext for obtaining the maximum delay, thus avoiding concrete action.
Why do I make this accusation? It is evident that the federal and provincial departments of agriculture have assembled most competent and professional staffs both in production and economic research and analysis. The cost-price squeeze has existed for so long that the term has become a cliche. Surely by now the high ranking officials have coordinated and marshalled all sorts of data about this cost-price squeeze, and possible approaches to ameliorate that condition. Do we, then, need some special task force to look into it?
I am suspicious that this government will use the task force to buy time as it did for example, regarding veterans pensions. I am not well versed in the functioning of that special committee on veterans pensions. I make reference to it for one specific purpose. Ever since I came here as a new federal member almost 18 months ago one of the things promised us almost from day to day, was that the Wood report was to be tabled very soon. It was to serve as a basis for the immediate adjustment of veterans pensions so as to reduce the disparity between those pensions and levels of income received by certain civil service classifications which were at parity decades ago. What has happened? Today, almost 18 months later, we are still waiting for that report. Veterans pensions remain far below parity and they lose more and more purchasing power each year.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
Any reasonable man can assume that at times there will be delays in submitting reports that last for a day, a week, a month, even for six months. But for a whole year? When there is such a delay in the presentation of a report which was promised us about 16 months ago and which we were then told was due any time, there is a credibility gap which cannot be closed. To put it in everyday language, who are the authorities trying to kid? They are using this report as an excuse
May 1G, 1967	COMMONS
to buy time because they have not been able to co-ordinate their policy thinking with regard to veterans pensions.
The fact is that decades ago veterans pensions were on a par with the salaries of certain job classifications, for example. This is no longer the case and now veterans pensions are as low as 60 per cent of that wage level. Is this acceptable? Obviously these veterans are at a disadvantage today in terms of purchasing power compared with their situation 10 or 20 years ago. Such discrepancies will arise in any dynamic society, in any moving economy, and this presents a problem which governments exist to cope with. It is one of the raisons d'etre of government but the administration opposite has not been acting effectively in this, their basic duty.
The cost of living has increased dramatically in the past two years. I know the Secretary of State for External Affairs and others who have made public comment on this subject in recent days would like Canadian citizens to believe that the rate of increase in the cost of living is lessening. Let us pause for a moment and examine the record of the government with regard to the rising cost of living syndrome. Last fall when the housewives were marching in chagrin and anger to protest the rising cost of living, the government was very accommodating and within a few days, not more than two weeks, it indicated that the whole serious subject would be referred to the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on consumer credit, a committee which then reconstituted itself somewhat into a committee on consumer prices.
There was nothing wrong with that move. It gave an opportunity to interested groups to make representations, file briefs and put forward submissions. It gave opportunities to members of parliament to probe with varying degrees of effectiveness into what appeared to be the major causes of these unacceptable increases in the cost of living. After deliberating for some time the committee handed in a number of interim reports.
I do not wish to be critical of that committee; in fact I am not. Nor do I wish to praise its efforts without reservation, because in my opinion in its work there was one serious omission. Adequate reference was not made to the very core of the subject which had been referred to it, namely the cause of the increase in prices. I know some of the chief accountants for the wholesalers and general
DEBATES	257
The Address-Mr. Schreyer stores appeared before the committee and were able to persuade certain members-not the majority, I hope-that the prices charged by wholesalers and chain store retailers were not unreasonable because after all, profits amounted to only 1 per cent of sales. The expert witnesses who use the profit to sales ratio are calculating to mislead.
I never could find any testimony in which specific reference was made to the level of profit in proportion to equity input or initial capital investment. Is it not disturbing to realize that there was no consistent pattern of questioning to invite these spokesmen to indicate their returns on equity input? I have here an Annual Report of a firm that is wholesaler to chain stores in the grocery business. I find that after seven years of operation-in the course of those seven years-the business enjoyed a profit of around 1J percent of sales, which is not much out of line with the figure mentioned by some of the other firms. This will not arouse much attention and some hon. members will say that is small profit. But here is the rub. In terms of return on equity input or investment the profit comes to a 29 per cent return on equity during each of the last four years of operation. I have it in mind to submit this particular report to the consumer affairs committee to find out, more than anything else, whether it is of a mind to ignore facts and figures of this kind.
[DOT] (1:00 p.m.)
Anyone who is at all involved in business and corporate affairs knows there is such a thing as a fair return, a reasonable return, an enticing return, a lucrative return, a return high enough to induce further investment. Similarly, however, any reasonable man should be ready to concede that there is such a thing as a unconscionable return. What will we do about it? Until such time as we have a price review board in this country certain sectors of the economy, certain wielders of economic power and influence, will be able to manipulate prices without much regard for public reaction.
The ladies were angry last year, and with cause. Their anger was diverted by the announcement that their whole area of complaint was being referred, that parliament was going to study it and presumably do something. Well, we are all members of parliament here, and I would like to arouse among my fellow members at least a trace of dissatisfaction with the work done so far and with the recommendations made by the committee on consumer affairs.
May 1G, 1967

The Address-Mr. Schreyer
We welcome the recommendation that a department of consumer affairs be appointed. Quite candidly I must say I am less enthusiastic about that proposition than most of my colleagues, though I am still on the positive side in supporting it. But one point of dissatisfaction is that the new department of consumer affairs will be combined with the administration of corporate affairs. One can just imagine which will get the short shrift when the chips are down. My colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North says it will be the elephant and mouse relationship, and I certainly do not disagree with his analogy.
I feel very much inclined to put more figures on the record with respect to this particular wholesale grocery chain store enterprise which over the past five years has been earning a return on equity input of the order of 28 per cent to 32 per cent, but it would be awkward to do so. However, I might add that during this period of time the equity itself has been substantially increased, not by additional subscriptions of new shares but simply by retained earnings from profits and all the while rather lavish dividends have been paid out-certainly on a scale high enough to have encouraged additional investment. The rub, though, was that these shares were not available to the public. At least they have not been available up until recently.
Putting it as an hypothesis, if in 1960 someone had bought 100 shares in this wholesale chain store enterprise he would have had to put up $200, the price then being $2 per share. In each subsequent year he would have received dividends as follows: in 1961, $5; in 1962, $7.50; in 1963, $7.50; in 1964, $10; in 1965, $12.50; in 1966, $18 and in 1967, $26, a total of $86.50 in dividends over six years on a capital input of $200. But that is only a small part of this story. The balance sheet reads like a fairy tale.
In addition to the dividend aspect there is of course the increase in shareholder equity simply because of profits kept as retained earnings and then being incorporated into assets held to the account of the company. I might made a correction at this point to say that the shares were put on the stock market two years ago, and the value of those 100 shares, bought for $200 in 1960, has fluctuated last year between $1,700 and $3,000. This shows the net worth and capital gains aspect of the question.
The more one looks at this kind of story the more one becomes convinced in respect to capital gains taxes, etc., that the Carter commission may well turn out to be one of the
[Mr. Schreyer.)
greatest and most worth-while royal commissions ever established in this country. There may be some aspects of the Carter commission report that will be unacceptable to the majority of the members of the house, but certainly no one will disagree that there are many features of it which are praiseworthy almost to the extreme, so praiseworthy that even Liberal candidates are calling for its implementation without qualification. Mr. Speaker, the
May 16, 1967	COMMONS
last speaker before the noon adjournment concluded his remarks by expressing regret that time did not permit him to cover a wider range of the subject matters raised in the speech from the throne. I find myself in somewhat the same predicament after reviewing the subjects in the speech from the throne which have been referred to during the past week of debate. Generally speaking, however, speeches have been related to two items, the need for further parliamentary reform, and reform of our constitution.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
Speeches in the latter category regarding the constitution have ranged all the way from the very thoughtful presentation of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) through to what I thought was the firebrand oratory of the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen). I was really pleased when the hon. member for Yukon spoke the other evening after his prolonged absence from the house. I noted that he had not lost his willingness to malign the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) or to distort historical facts. I prepared a rather lengthy rebuttal to the remarks of the hon. member for Yukon but since he spoke my attention has been focused rather on the turmoil which exists in the New Democratic party on this subject. I was not concerned the other evening when they presented a subamendment to the effect that there were two nations in Canada. They include this theory in their constitution which they have distributed in the province of Quebec for some years. They easily get around the question of the two-nation theory by emphasizing that of course they recognize the existence of two nations in Canada but only in the cultural sense and not in the political sense.
From the result of the vote the other evening it is obvious that no one took the subamendment too seriously because everyone knew full well that within the next day or so some socialist spokesman for the New Democratic party would tour the country explaining that they really did not mean there should be two nations in this country but that they were speaking of two nations in the cultural sense. I was more concerned when I read some of the remarks of the leader of that party when he spoke over the week end at a convention in Quebec and formally announced that his party now recognizes a special status for the province of Quebec. I intend to discuss that special status in the short time available to me. I might also review the speech which I had anticipated someone
DEBATES	259
The Address-Mr. Mackasey would make in the next day or two after that convention. In this case it was the speech of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) who quickly and efficiently placed on the record the interpretation of the New Democratic party concerning specifically what Quebec's special status is, at least as they understand it.

The hon. member for Verdun is not very good at subtleties. The hon. member has just emphasized what I started to say. In that party its members find many opportunities to say one thing in Quebec and another thing in the rest of Canada. They go to Quebec and say they recognize two nations. Then they say they do not mean exactly that there are two nations but rather two nations in a cultural sense. The point is that the time has passed when the New Democratic party can go into Quebec and preach one doctrine and go to Vancouver and preach another.
Before I get too far into this subject I should like to say something about parliamentary reform. I hope no one interprets my remarks as an indication that I am against parliamentary reform. On the contrary. I think most of the rules and regulations which were introduced, particularly under the previous Speaker, have done much to speed up the deliberations of the House of Commons. This is necessary in order to get through the house the amount of legislation which is before us.
One thing, however, which has provoked me a little is that in our obsession to increase the efficiency of the committees we do so at the expense of the House of Commons. Not too long ago I was upset when the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) made a very important statement on Viet Nam in the house when there were precisely 31 members present. Where were the other members? They were attending committees such as the food and drugs committee, the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs and others.

speechtext:
I have not met a thinner-skinned bunch in this house than the socialists. There must be some ways and means to protect the House of Commons. One problem which we must face in respect of the committee system is that all too frequently we grant permission for committees to sit while the house is sitting. In the final analysis this is a house of debate and unless we make certain there is a sufficient quorum in the house at all times, for matters to be debated efficiently then, as the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) said, one of the basic principles of democracy will disappear, the right to stand up in the House of Commons and debate the issues of the day.
The hon. member for Yukon mentioned the two-nation theory. While he appeared to attack the N.D.P. for the two-nation theory he laid the blame directly on the shoulders of the Prime Minister. I did a little searching in the meantime to find out what noted parliamentarian or politician first discussed two nations in a cultural sense. Not too long ago-100 years-Sir John A. Macdonald said this about our French speaking Canadians:
Treat them as a nation and they will act as a free people do-generously. Call them a faction and they become factious.
Lord Durham stated in his writings that he found "two nations warring in the bosom of a single state." Eugene Forsey, writing in the Canadian Journal of Economics and Political Science, said:
Canada is both two nations and one: two nations in the ethnic, cultural, sociological sense:	one
nation in the political, legal, constitutional sense.
Perhaps the greatest authority of all is the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) who on July 2, 1963, as found on page 2442 of Hansard, said:
When confederation took place a new nation was created in the partnership of two basic nationalities.
This is the reason I could not become too upset the other evening when the New Democratic party, in an attempt to infiltrate the province of Quebec, advanced the two-nations concept as a subamendment. I knew it would be only a matter of time before one of them would get up and say that they are

emphasizing culture, as the hon. member for Springfield did a few moments ago.
I am more interested in the special status the leader the New Democratic party seeks for the province of Quebec. I am a resident of the province of Quebec. Contrary to public opinion there are more English speaking Quebeckers at the moment than there are people in some of the other provinces. There are over a million of us. Quebec does not need special status. If the leader of the N.D.P. had said that Quebec is different from the other provinces I would endorse such a statement. Certainly it is different. It is the homeland of one of the founding races of this country. It is populated by the great majority of French speaking Canadians. It is different culturally, linguistically and in many other ways. Its civil code is different.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
But Quebec does not need special status in 1967 or in 1970 to attain its full maturity under confederation. What it needs is respect for the constitution by other governments and respect for the constitution could have very well been exercised by the New Democratic party during the 16 years that it formed the government in Saskatchewan. What did that party do in those years for the French speaking minority? It did nothing. It was a disgrace then and it is still a disgrace. When the leader of the New Democratic party comes to the province of Quebec, as he did last week end, and says that Quebec must have a special status in this country so as to survive, he is fooling no one. In this day of modern communications, to preach one message in Quebec and another in Vancouver will have its repercussions, as the socialists will find out.
Of course I was not invited to that particular gathering of would-be socialists, and I had to rely on the Montreal Star of Monday, May 15, to find out what happened there. According to this newspaper the leader of the New Democratic party said:
-the position of the N.D.P. "is that the sensible and long-range solution lies in the constitutional recognition of the fact that Quebec is not a province like the other provinces and that its cultural needs and objectives cannot be fulfilled, except that they are met by special arrangements."
What are the special arrangements which the leader of the N.D.P. proposes for Quebec? He did not outline them. All he did was voice platitudes. So I waited, knowing full well that within a day or two a senior spokesman of the N.D.P. would get up in the House of Commons and attempt to put on the record a
May 16, 1967

message diametrically opposed to that of his leader, so that out west the members of that party could quote Hansard and in Quebec they could quote the Montreal Star. Sure enough, the hon. member for Greenwood made just such a speech on May 15. Again I can only go by Hansard because I was not here to hear him. But I read his speech not once but two or three times. His words, as found on page 203 of Hansard, are very noble and are bound to please the most nationalistic of Canadians. He said:
We ought to entrench in our constitution a constitutional bill of rights. We have at present a bill of rights which was passed by parliament, but its inadequacy is obvious. It does not apply to provincial legislatures, and may be repealed by parliament at any time-
This is precisely what the Prime Minister said earlier. I agree with it. It is also exactly the same message as was contained in brief of the different trade unions from the province of Quebec. However, farther on in the same column he went on to say:
The other point to be borne in mind is whether it is wise, in our revised constitution, or necessary to allow Quebec a special status.
Note, he is beginning to doubt the wisdom of the very statement that his leader made over the week end. The headline in the newspaper to which I referred reads: "Special Status Avoids Turmoil". Then he said:
The expression "special status" is very general, and it is necessary to be precise when dealing with it, and I propose later in my remarks to define more precisely what we in this party mean when we say we are in favour of a special status for Quebec.
I read this with anticipation. I said to myself, here is one member of the socialist party who is going to tell us what he means by a special status for the province of Quebec. Should Quebec become an associate state in a two-nation confederation? Will Quebec go one way and the rest of Canada another, meeting periodically to split the budget? I read on, anticipating the hon. member for Greenwood would explain to us what he means by special status.
Incidentally, one thing that intrigues me is that members of the New Democratic party, who never tire of quoting Sweden as an example and whose philosophy is based on a strong central government, now pretend to be the greatest exponents of decentralization. But here is what the hon. member for Greenwood had to say:
To this end we believe that federal authority must be preserved in such fields as credit, banking, investment, monetary and fiscal policy, tariffs and transportation, to name a few only.

According to him these are the areas in which the federal authority must remain supreme. After removing all these fields from provincial jurisdiction, one assumed that he had reached the area of special status which, according to the leader of the New Democratic party, Quebec should have if Canada is to survive. Instead the hon. member for Greenwood said the following, and we hear this from a spokesman of a party which is advocating decentralization:
We have been concerned about the gradual erosion of federal powers in the fields I mentioned which has become apparent in federal-provincial conferences over the past few years.
In other words, the hon. member for Greenwood, at the same time as his leader was making a speech in the province of Quebec advocating a special status for Quebec and increased provincial jurisdiction in these particular areas, was preparing a speech to be delivered in the House of Commons in which he bemoaned the fact that too much federal jurisdiction in the areas I have just mentioned had been transferred to the province of Quebec. Perhaps it was time that this authority be removed from Quebec and from other provinces and returned to the central government he suggested. I do not necessarily disagree with his principle. I am merely pointing out the hypocrisy of his message. He says one thing and his leader says another.
Since the hon. member for Greenwood has decided that jurisdiction in these particular fields should not be transferred to the provinces, and therefore to Quebec, I thought he perhaps meant that Quebec should assume a special status in other areas. This is what he said at page 204 of Hansard:
It is desirable to have federal control in fields such as family alowances, non-contributory old age pensions and the like. There are some fields such as hospitalization and health services where the present system of provincial administration and partial federal financing works well-
So far he has not advocated one single, solitary change in the present constitution. He went on to say:
-and where it should be retained with great advantage in transferability of benefits throughout Canada. Here also the federal contribution helps equalize the burden as between provinces.
In other words, the hon. member for Greenwood is advocating precisely what we are advocating, namely, that the have provinces help the have-not provinces. What is revolutionary about this? Realizing that he had not said anything endorsing a special
May 16, 1967

The Address-Mr. Mackasey status, he went on to support his argument by saying:
-it is merely a recognition of the facts of life, namely that people with a special culture of their own are entitled to retain complete control, if they so desire, over matters intimately connected with that culture such as education.
Who has ever denied the province of Quebec control over education? If for the past 30, 40 or 100 years, Quebec chose to put emphasis on a classical education, that was the province's prerogative and privilege and nobody has tried to interfere with it. One thing that needs to be done is for parliament to define education one of these days. But that is not what the hon. member for Greenwood said. He went on to say in his dramatic way that we should recognize the rights of the provinces in the field of education. This is one field where the provinces have been and should always be supreme, but since there were no tangible suggestions in the rest of his speech I suppose the hon. member had to say something.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
The hon. member was not even willing to give this to Quebec without some restriction because he goes on to say:
On the other hand, it must be recognized that it is the people in the other nine provinces who ought to be most insistent that Quebec should have a special status and that federal intervention should not be restricted to the level desired by Quebec.
How are you going to tell Quebec that it has autonomy in the field of education and a special status at the same time, but that the federal government can intervene at a level not necessarily desired by Quebec?
It is contended by the member that in fiscal, tariff, transportation, banking and credit, and investment matters the federal government must remain supreme. This is what the hon. member for Greenwood contends. The federal government must remain supreme also in the field of vocational allowances, old age pensions and the like he says. In so far as hospitalization and health services are concerned, joint participation seems to work well according to the hon. member for Greenwood and should not be altered. The only area which he concedes to the province is the area of education which it has always had.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Pepin), who is an expert in this field and has made many speeches throughout the country on federal-provincial relations and the constitution, intervened. I should like

to refer to his question which is recorded on page 205 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, if I may I should like to direct a question to the hon. member. Am I right in thinking that special status as he defines it implies no change in the present constitutional situation toward a further decentralization in favour of Quebec particularly?

speechtext:
I do not think it implies any change.
Of course it does not. Knowing that his leader has come out with his two-nations concept in the province of Quebec and had advocated a special status in confederation for the province of Quebec, the hon. member for Greenwood rushes into parliament to correct what his leader has said. If the leader of the New Democratic party believes Quebec should have a special status, then let him tour the country and say so. He does not do so. I can understand the problem, and it is a serious one. He goes to Montreal on the week end and finds that the Quebec wing of the New Democratic party has adopted a resolution stating that the province of Quebec is supreme in international affairs. The province can make what agreements it wants on any level with foreign powers such as France, Belgium and perhaps even Ireland. The leader of the New Democratic party on Saturday had to rely on his troops to defeat this resolution which had been adopted by the Quebec wing.
I ask the 19 or 20 members of the gallant little band in the corner, whose philosophy do you follow, that preached by your leader in Quebec or that preached in the House of Commons by the hon. member for Greenwood? Do you accept the resolution of the Quebec wing to the effect that Quebec can make international treaties or do you accept the philosophy of your leader which denies this privilege? In other words, Mr. Speaker, the New Democrats are on the horns of a dilemma. They forget that this is 1967 and you cannot go into Quebec with one philosophy and to Vancouver with another. This practice is catching up with them and I am not sorry. They have been playing with both sides of the coin too long. Once upon a time the leader of the New Democratic party may have been able to get people to stand up in the House of Commons and refute what he said outside the House of Commons in the hope that these statements could assume equal validity across Canada. However, this cannot be done today.
There is nothing in the speech by the hon. member for Greenwood that defines what the special status for Quebec is to be. I suggest to
May 16, 1967	COMMONS
the members of the New Democratic party that the unity of Canada is too sacred to be subjected to party politics. You have to be consistent. If you believe, and I do not, that Quebec needs a special status to remain in confederation, then say so in the house as well as outside the house. Let the leader of the New Democratic party take advantage of this debate or some other occasion to get up in the house and state what is to be the special status for the province of Quebec. French speaking Canadians do not want to be isolated from the mainstream of Canada. They do not have to be. They have something to offer and they have offered it. This is manifest to anyone who takes the trouble to observe. Their contribution to this country has been as great as that of the English speaking people of this country. They have supplied not only a prime minister and a governor general but the leader of the army and the head of the Supreme Court of Canada. Leaders in the fields of culture and science are found in great numbers amongst the French speaking people. They do not need a special status to contribute to this nation, only an opportunity and a climate devoid of intolerance and prejudice.
The province of Quebec has complete control of the field of education as well as other areas outlined in the constitution. All Quebec wants and deserves is respect for the constitution as it now exists. The only sensible suggestion which has come out of the House of Commons in relation to this Whole problem has been the one made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) the other evening and also on several occasions by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin). What we need to do in this house is to thresh out a bill of rights for this country, without denying the one in existence. It was a milestone in the history of Canada when the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) instituted a Bill of Rights for this country. It is one of which we should be proud and it is above partisanship. However, we want to know what provincial rights and municipal rights are, not merely the rights of individuals.
When the Prime Minister stated provincial leaders should meet later this year to define our objectives before we find a way to amend the constitution, or to add to it or remove the redundant sections, he was talking common sense. Newspapers close to the scene such as the Montreal Star know this. It is an English language newspaper in the heart of French Canada, one that knows the problems of the 27053-18J

The Montreal Star is a newspaper which has always been responsible when discussing the problems of the constitution and the need for changes in it. In an editorial dated Saturday, May 13, 1967, this newspaper states that the Prime Minister suggested a most sensible and pragmatic way to approach the very complex problem of confederation. The editorial continues:
The Prime Minister is, to begin with at any rate, against the formal, committee type conference which leads only to a public display of individual political postures. He will resist any "constitutional leap in the dark."
But he offered what seems to us a highly sensitive first step which could be taken by all without impinging on the particular positions of any. Mr. Pearson hoped the first move in the constitutional field could be an agreement by all the premiers on a common bill of rights. Such provincial bills would be based on the existing federal bill which will always be, as Mr. Pearson noted gracefully, associated with the name of Mr. Diefenbaker. Then he continued:
"Surely before we can seriously hope to agree on structural changes, we should endeavour to agree, federally and provincially, on a statement of common values and on a declaration of our basic individual and collective rights as Canadians."
The first positive step that should come out of that conference, Mr. Speaker, is to make the district of Ottawa truly representative of the two founding races of this country. Politician after politician, in this house and outside, condemns the potholes in Ottawa. This is not what we should condemn. We should condemn the unilingual aspect of this area. We should make the Ottawa district truly representative of the two founding races of this country. If we cannot come to that conclusion as a result of one of these conferences, then how in God's holy name are we going to agree on changing the constitution or any part of it? This is a test of good will.

Mr. Speaker, I shall not sound a discordant note in this general harmony, and I shall maintain the tradition of this house in congratulating the mover of the address in reply to the speech from the throne (Mr. Jamieson) and the seconder (Mr. Cote).
If my information is correct, Mr. Speaker, I am told that the mover of the address in reply to the speech from the throne has made his maiden speech in this house. In this case, I can tell him that his first try proved to be a master stroke, and I hope that he will make many speeches like this one, so that I myself may benefit from this lesson in eloquence.
Now Mr. Speaker, if I may, I shall comment some of the items contained in the speech from the throne and I will quote word for word:
Our country was not founded in 1867. It is far more deeply rooted in time than that. But, one hundred years ago, our predecessors-men of many races, creeds and tongues-embarked upon a great exercise in statecraft of which we, today, are the trustees. They laid the foundations. They anchored them in a fundamental sense of unity that generations of conflict had taught was vital to the common weal. With this realization they erected a structure of government for the freedom, welfare, and prosperity of all who might come in time to inhabit this land. They built according to a federal plan because they knew that unity, with cultural and regional diversity could be harnessed to a positive and enriching role in no other way.
And further on.
The path of confederation has been beset with great difficulties-some natural, some inevitable and some of our own making.
I gather, Mr. Speaker, that it was those two items that the leader of the Ralliement Creditiste (Mr. Caouette) wished to comment especially in his speech of May 11 last in this house. I will quote word for word the following, which appears on page 76 of the May 11 Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, everyone knows that I am a Frenchspeaking Canadian and that I fight for the recognition of French Canadians throughout Canada. It is indeed a duty for me to say that I have had a friendly reception in all those provinces: I might even say that I have had a warmer welcome in the western universities than in the university of Montreal, in my own provinces of Quebec.
That is saying a good deal, Mr. Speaker.
And these people out west, these young students, these farmers or whoever they are, are most hospitable. We are welcomed like kings in those provinces. Even if these young people do not speak our language, they are eager to welcome us, to hear our problems, to learn to know us, to know
[Mr. Deputy Speaker.1
what we want and who we are. It was most interesting to meet these people, irrespective of political affiliations, as Canadians from a province other than theirs.
Mr. Speaker, although some of our opponents make unkind remarks about the leader of the Ralliement Creditiste, it must be recognized that he does make allowances and gives everyone his due. In this connection, I take it upon myself to repeat a sentence spoken by our leader, and I quote:
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
-and I would even say that I was made more welcome by the western universities than by the university of Montreal which is in my own province of Quebec.
Just to corroborate that statement and that tribute, I will relate an incident I witnessed, as did several of my colleagues, when the government invited us to visit Expo and Habitat on April 8 last.
Frankly, Mr. Speaker, as a French-speaking Canadian, I was far from edified. If the house will allow me, I will describe the experience several members and senators, accompanied by their wives, went through.
We were greeted warmly at Expo, particularly by the commissioner general who, when we set foot on the grounds, shook hands with us and smiled broadly at us. But I guess it was only to make us accept meekly what was to come. In fact, when the time came for Expo's commissioner general to introduce the hon. members and senators to those present, he found nothing better than to make his whole speech in English from beginning to end. I am not holding it against my English friends who were made so welcome. But we, the French Canadians, were ignored to such an extent that, while the commissioner general was speaking, my wife who was with me on that occasion asked me: Does that man not speak French? I will not repeat the reflection I made to my wife, because I do want to respect this house of parliament, but let it be known that my words were not in praise of the commissioner general.
Mr. Speaker, I want to point out to my colleagues that this happened last April 8, in the very heart of the province of Quebec, in the second French city of the world, Montreal, which, this year, plays host to some 60 exhibiting countries on Terre des Hommes. That treatment we cannot be proud of. As a snub, as a rebuff, as a stinging slap in the face of this country's French Canadians, it could not have been better. For my part, I
