call that the unkindest cut of all. Fortunately there are contrasts which are a little more encouraging and comforting.
During the hockey finals between the Montreal Canadiens and the Toronto Maple Leafs-we noted this fact right here and, as I said, I am not criticizing anyone, even though several members stayed away from the house to watch television; I readily admit that I cheated myself-I noticed, along with several other members, I am sure, that before every game, both in Toronto and in Montreal, the national anthem "O Canada" was played.
Last Sunday, Mr. Speaker, I attended the two consecutive ceremonies on parliament hill in honour of the fathers of confederation.
And after each of those ceremonies, the national anthem "O Canada" was sung in English and in French.
I think that everything is completely changed. Those who were charged not so long ago with fanatical intolerance are now giving us a good lesson of patriotism and national pride. And some people will then talk of separatism, independentism; some will bellow to everyone that the last hundred years of Canadian confederation have been one hundred years of injustice for French Canadians, and all sorts of slogans like that. To these people who fish in troubled waters, I will suggest that respect is not commanded but imposed.
Mr. Speaker, I recollect the kind exhortations that the gracious Queen of England and of all commonwealth countries made to us on her last trip to Canada. After having suggested and urged that the two great nations making up this country, which have inherited the most refined of western civilizations whose influence has been felt by almost all the peoples in the world, work towards unity and mutual understanding, she summed up her thoughts as follows. Listen well, my dear colleagues; I hope this exhortation by the Queen of England will remain deeply imprinted in your minds:
Our patriotism must never lead us to forget the patriotism of others.
That is the challenge presented to us by the next hundred years of our Canadian confederation. This challenge we can and will meet.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Now, I shall quote another part of the speech from the throne, which I shall comment briefly:
In 1867-
That was a hundred years ago.
-it was possible to think of the public responsibility primarily in terms of state responsibility. The new challenges, which we must and will meet, require the involvement of the whole society and the effort of all our people. In this time of fastchanging dimensions, the central concern of Canadian society must be the well-being of each individual, so that, regardless of his place or station of birth, he will have an equal chance to realize his full potential in the economic, social, political and cultural sense. A country is a home; it must be built and furnished for the good life of its people.
Do you not think that is beautiful?
With our forefathers, the fight was against the immense odds of nature on our half of this continent.
That is the heritage our forefathers have passed on to us so that we may live better.
Today, the main struggle is against social, injustice, against cultural mediocrity, against spiritual stagnation and against all forms of Intolerance.
Mr. Speaker, at this point of my remarks, I shall try mainly to emphasize the economic value of the individual, of the Canadian citizen. The first part of the Canadian Bill of Rights reads as follows:
[DOT]-it is recognized and declared that in Canada there have existed and shall continue to exist without discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour, religion or sex, the following human rights and fundamental freedoms, namely,
(a)	the right of the individual to life, liberty, security of the person and enjoyment of property, and the right not to be deprived thereof except by due process of law;
(b)	the right of the individual to equality before the law and the protection of the law;
(c)	freedom of religion;
(d)	freedom of speech;
(e)	freedom of assembly and association; and
(f)	freedom of the press.
Mr. Speaker, in 1960, when the Conservative party was in power, two Liberal members at least asked for the addition of the economic rights and freedoms to those mentioned above. The intervention, at that time, of the hon. member who is now a minister in this cabinet, appears in Hansard of July 5, 1960.1 quote:
Yes, political freedoms are referred to in this bill, but it is not as a result giving to the citizen a greater security of enjoyment than what is now provided for in the law. Our legal liberties are partly mentioned but not our economic liberties, except for section 2	(a) referring to property.
There is no mention nor is there any declaration of the conviction that must stand behind even these newly conceived rights. It may be that it is difficult to put into a charter like this what we mean by economic rights; but at a time when society is evolving and when the poltical philosophy of every party in this house subscribes to the view of full employment, is it unfair or extravagant to suggest in this twentieth century
May 16, 1967

The Address-Mr. Simard
that we have the right to place alongside our political freedoms, with no less effect, those rights that affect the economic well-being of the citizen?
Then further he goes on to say:
I say that a bill of rights is not complete that does not take into account these economic rights. Nor does this bill deal with liberty in what one might call its human rights or egalitarian sense; such things as fair employment practice laws, fair accommodation laws, equal pay for women laws-
He did not even forget the women.
-all laws which emancipate women, the right to election, the right to medical care, the right to disability pensions, and so on. Are we to say that these are not rights? Are we to say that in the objectives we have placed for ourselves we are not to regard these as legitimate aspirations?
Mr. Speaker, in 1960 another Liberal member corroborated the statement and the stand taken by his colleague. I quote:
Furthermore, the Criminal Code provides for arrest for failure to provide of any head of family who does not meet that obligation. If it is true that, for any obligation which is placed on the shoulders of a citizen, the state has a duty towards him, if it is true that the legislator imposed upon the Canadian citizen that obligation to feed and maintain his family, I think that it is only fair and legitimate that the same legislator should give to that man the means to fulfil that obligation. I submit that a bill of rights that does not take into account these economic rights is not complete at all.
The two Liberal members were then criticizing the introduction of the Canadian Bill of Rights by the Conservatives.
Those claims are based on section 22 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and can be summed up so:
Everyone has the right to life, liberty and security of person, and enjoyment of property.
Those are rights the Social Credit party wants for every single Canadian citizen. Here is a declaration of principle as stated by the Canadian Social Credit Association:
Social Credit firmly believes that the individual is the most important factor in organized society. Because he is a divinely created being with spiritual, mental and physical needs and potentialities, he has inalienable rights which must be respected and preserved.
Mr. Speaker, if I may, I will now add a few comments.
What is Canada? Canada is a country which comprises mainly-let this be emphasized- 20,400,000 human beings, 4,800,000 families and 400,000 corporations.
The 4,800,000 families of one or more persons live in the 4,800,000 housing units or castles; in addition, there are slums which

one can see, when visiting our country, Canada.
Tremendous prosperity, inhuman distribution. Let us correct the situation right now, instead of losing time blaming the persons responsible, instead of looking for guilty parties, for wrong-doers. Let us suddenly become benefactors of our own humanity in Canada.
Each of the 265 Canadian members of parliament was elected by the people who live in each of Canada's ridings. The companies do not vote. Therefore, the companies do not elect the members of parliament. Why be afraid of the companies once we are elected?
The companies are only institutions made up of groups of human beings, but the companies themselves do not exist, are not alive, do not vote. They are the instruments of production or administration of the material, intellectual or spiritual goods and services which meet the needs of the people.
There are in Canada 265 members of parliament and 26 ministers, of whom only one is Minister of Finance. If Canada's prosperity depends on all the people and all the companies of Canada, the distribution of that prosperity rests mainly with the Minister of Finance, the 25 ministers and the 265 members of parliament.
If production is abundant in 1967, there is no reason why distribution in 1967 should be a failure and a disaster for the great majority of the population. What is produced in 1967 should be distributed that year.
Production takes place within our present monetary, economic and political systems. Distribution must therefore be properly done within the framework of the same monetary, economic and political systems.
There is no need for a new constitution, new political parties, another election, new departments or new instruments of production or administration.
What is lacking is a simple pressure adjustment in the money circulation, in the present capitalist system of Canada-

Mr. Speaker, taking part in the debate in reply to the speech from the throne on our hundredth anniversary imposes a requirement on every member to review the last 100 years of the
May 16, 1967	COMMONS
history of this country and to try to project the lessons of those years into the future problems facing Canadians. As a result of my consideration of this matter 1 have decided to make my centennial remarks on the subject of three choices for Canada.
Before I embark on a discussion of these three alternative courses of economic policy for Canada I want to preface my remarks by saying that as one reads the debates of 100 years ago it is amazing to find the similarity to the discussion we hear in this debate today. Today I had the privilege of listening to a Liberal member from the great city of Montreal, representing the constituency of Verdun, who was taking issue with the remarks made by an N.D.P. member from Toronto in the house the other day. Just now we have listened to a member from rural Quebec outlining some of the problems he sees. The remarks made today by these distinguished members of the House of Commons can all be duplicated in the debates of 100 years ago. Instead of the term "special status for Quebec", in those days members used the term "co-ordinate sovereignty". It is the same thing, I suppose, as the phrase used by the members of the N.D.P., and I would expect that 100 years from now it is conceivable that the debate at that time will have a new phrase but the subject will be the same.
Having said that I want to move on to the question of what were some of the issues that forced our forebears 100 years ago to accept the concept of a federal system of government in this great sprawling country. Certainly the need for defence against the victorious armies of the northern states was paramount in their minds. Certainly the depression in what we now call the Atlantic provinces was a great spur to the delegates from that area to accept another form of government. Above all, I would think that the political stalemate in the two Canadas we now call Quebec and Ontario was a reason for men with widely divergent views to come to a common conclusion.
In our review of the debates of 100 years ago we are lucky now to have available to us a history written by Canadians. To me personally it was always almost an intolerable insult that Canadians never had an authentic source of their history to which they could refer. We have been forced over the last 60-odd years to use an English history, the Cambridge History of Canada, for the authentic documentation of our story, but as part of
DEBATES	267
The Address-Mr. Hamilton the centennial observations the government of which I was a member had, I believe, the foresight to ask our historians in Canada to prepare for the first time some form of authentic Canadian history written by Canadians. This centenary series is now being published. It will consist of 17 volumes and I expect they will all be published this year.
I am going to ask the permission of the house to include the list of these volumes in my speech as part of the written record of this second debate dealing with confederation.
I would like to take the time to read just a few of the names, but suffice it to say that the Canadian centenary series is headed by Dr. Morton, the executive editor, who was professor of history at the University of Manitoba. Dr. Creighton from Toronto is the associate editor. These two men correlated the work of all the specialists on the various segments of our history.
The volume I hold in my hand is volume No. 12, written by Dr. Morton on the subject of confederation. It deals with the years 1857 to 1873, a 16-year period. It is not written in a light reading form. It is a straightforward account of what happened. I think that every member of parliament now and for many years to come should have this 17-volume history of his country in his library at home and possibly in his library in his office. Certainly every school teacher who has been given the responsibility of teaching the history of his country should have these volumes available for reference. I personally, and I hope on behalf of all Canadians, want to thank these distinguished historians for giving their time, almost for nothing, to provide us for the first time with an authentic history of our country written by Canadians.
Rather than read all their names and the subjects they dealt with I wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether I could have the permission of the house to have a list of these authors and their subjects incorporated as part of my address at this point in my speech.

speechtext:
Coming to my subject, three choices for Canada, I wish to say that Canada today is a far different country from what it was in 1867. We have learned a great deal in the last century not only about our own geography and our resources but about the technology of government. For instance, with our modern knowledge of monetary and fiscal policies it is thought that never again will the countries of the industrial world have to endure great depressions such as those that were characteristic of our economy in the last century. This knowledge must be utilized not only by the members of the federal parliament but by all legislatures in the world to make certain that the growth rate of our countries can be maintained at a pace that balances full employment with the best possible stabilized price structure. It is on this basis that one can, as a parliamentarian, now set oneself clearly defined targets and hope to achieve them.
If one examines the growth rate of our great neighbouring country to the south in the last 100 years and particularly notices the last few years one finds that it has tended to have an annual growth rate of about 4 per cent per year. Then if one examines our own growth rate since 1961 and even earlier and works out an average, it is very clear that economically at this moment in our history we should be setting ourselves a target which past experience shows we can achieve to get maximum employment and stabilized prices at the same time.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
I want to suggest as this target, which I have arrived at with great timidity in trying to find something that is practical, that we as the Canadian legislative group responsible for the economic health of our country should this year on our one hundredth birthday set an average growth rate of 6 per cent per year. If we can maintain our growth rate between 5 per cent and 7 per cent over the next two or three decades then Canadians will know that
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Richard).]
in comparison with the United States growth rate, which I think will average about 4 per cent based on past experience, on a per capita basis we will be equal in wealth to our neighbours to the south. I think an average of 6 per cent is a reasonable, practical and possible rate to achieve. This is an objective we can very well set ourselves and we can have confidence in our ability to reach this target.
If we have the confidence we have the resources. The inventory of our resources is much clearer now than it was ten years ago. We certainly have the energy, and the inventory of potential energy resources is much clearer than ten years ago. We also have some knowledge of our water resources and our basic resources both renewable and nonrenewable. With this energy, water and resources there is no reason we cannot maintain a growth rate average of 6 per cent which will make us on a per capita basis the wealthiest nation in the world in the next quarter century. Surely that should be our target.
It is passing strange that with the Canadian characteristic of lack of confidence in ourselves we have to learn from the United States that all these things are possible. We have to learn this from reports such as the Paley report of 1952 and the Landsberg report of 1963. With our resources, energy and water and the targets I have mentioned we have the potential to become the most wealthy nation in the world. That is the key of my message for 1967. If my colleague from Queens, Prince Edward Island is correct, that no one today will pay any attention to what I say, I hope that 100 years from now those people who read the record of what has been said during this debate on the anniversary of our first century will realize that these remarks have been vindicated.
To achieve this growth rate we have to make one major decision. We must decide which of three economic courses to follow. Let me outline these courses in a succinct way. We may choose the course of continen-talism, we can go back to the old traditional policies of restrictive nationalism, or we can choose the course of expansionist nationalism. Those are the three courses.
Continentalism is a phrase used to describe the conviction held by many Canadians over the last 100 years that it is the ultimate destiny of Canada to become part of an economic union with the United States and eventually part of a political union. Great Canadians have held this view and sincere Canadians hold this view today, with the same sincerity
May 16, 1967

The Address-Mr. Hamilton
I trust as those who held it in the past. One of the greatest Canadians ever to grace this Canadian assembly, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, all through his life as a young radical, as a growing power in the political world, and finally as a senior statesman held the view that the ultimate destiny of our country was some form of union with the United States. Only once or twice in his political career when he was angry with the United States about one or two things did he ever veer from this view.
This view is held by many people today in the Liberal party, as was demonstrated last September in Ottawa at the policy convention. At that great policy convention the majority of Liberal delegates indicated with full sincerity that they were in favour of a commercial union with the United States. This view is held sincerely by many people. I do not know that all people in Canada want to accept it, but I know there is no question about the feelings of those of us in this part of the house who call ourselves Progressive Conservatives.
The second choice, restrictive nationalism, has been the traditional policy of both Liberals and Conservatives for the last 80 years. This is the policy under which we try to build walls around our country to protect our workers and our business elements and to make sure that the level of living in this country is reasonably fair to all segments. It was in this traditional policy of restrictive nationalism that we built our industry, but we now know it has become obsolete and out of date over the last quarter of a century.
At the present time this type of policy is followed intensively by one of the Toronto members on the government side, whom I admire for his sincerity. I suppose there are many members in this place who support him. The use of the phrase "restrictive nationalism" may be argued, but generally the feeling is the same, that the people who hold to the choice of restrictive protection are accurately described as restrictive nationalists. They follow this course for good motives. They do not want to see Canada drifting because of a lack of action into an economic part of the United States and eventually a political part of that country. Those of us who are nationalists can admire those people in all parties who support restrictive nationalism because they do so for a good purpose.
There is a third choice, and that choice is expansionist nationalism. It does not depend just on flag waving or on drifting along and
letting things happen. It depends on a government which believes there is a place on the north half on this continent for a country that is peculiarly our own. The word which describes that kind of a government is "dynamic". Such a government must meet the pressures of modern corporate capitalism. This is universal, not just peculiar to one country or one continent. It exists all over the world as a type of economic organization which sees no boundary lines and pays no attention to morals or national aspirations.
In a system which produces so much wealth what are we as Canadians to do? Some would turn back the clock and try to deny these benefits to our people. Others want to succumb to them and say that if we were all to become the same all over the world this would be an end in itself worthy to be desired. There are others who say, let us make use of the larger producing capacities of this system and yet, because we are the sovereign people in this parliament, live up to moral principles by developing in a moral way those things to satisfy all forms of basic need of life, and above all to serve the interests of the group.
The group to which I refer is made up of those who call themselves Canadians. There is a place in mankind's struggle for a better and better life for the group. This is not a world in which everything comes down to the individual benefit. There is a place for the family, for community values and for a group such as a nation. You do not necessarily have to be bilingual or eloquent; you just need a mere consciousness that you are a group slightly different from other groups. This is not bad; it is good. It inspires people to do many things that the theory of individualism cannot inspire a person to do.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I hold the view that no culture can survive based on the theory that as long as an individual gets the most for himself the sum total is a good society. I reject that theory of complete individualism. We use it, I know, to get economic development, but at the same time I know there must exist along with that the awareness that there is a value in group loyalty and group discipline. I am a Canadian. This may be a miserable culture on the northern half of this continent but, by Jove, it is our own and I think we should work to maintain it. I do not think we should build walls between the free parts of the world and the others. I do not think we will achieve this group consciousness by sitting
May 16, 1967

The Address-Mr. Hamilton here and doing nothing. I believe we can build this country only if we work dynamically, positively and constructively to do so.
Therefore there is a third choice, expansionism at home and abroad. We all know, however, that we have slipped a longways down the slippery slope of union with the United States. First of all, the natural economic structure of our two countries has tied us together so that we are like Siamese twins who cannot separate without mortal harm to one or both. We know that during the last war we joined our war efforts and this has pushed us once more into the arms of a continental economic system. It disturbs me to watch the development of my country and see a failure to realize opportunities to be positive, dynamic and expansionist in building up the country. I bleed a little for my fellow Canadians.
What are the techniques of this dynamic positive expansionism? I will not recite all of the things of the past but let me mention a few. In Canada we must have a consciousness of a development policy for our resources so that regions are deliberately built up when they fall behind. In Canada we must have a deliberate policy to help those segments of the population which do not share reasonably equally in the wealth of this nation.
As I said earlier, to achieve these ends we must use our monetary and fiscal know-how which we have accumulated over the last 15 or 20 years. That would be a speech by itself. We must realize that our trade techniques are tying us more and more to the industrial world and are making the gulf between the newly developed nations and the industrial wealthy nations greater. We deliberately, dynamically, positively and constructively must build those institutions to bridge that gulf.
I spoke on this matter on October 8, 1964, I believe. If anyone wishes to go back and read some of my proposals he will find them in that speech. We must think deliberately of how by positive means we can get more processing in Canada. I might mention an example. Last year a Canadian company wanted to bring more western gas into eastern Canada and reduce the price below the level of the United States price. This would have meant more industry, lower costs in Canada and more businesses without any artificial restriction. This is the reason I took the stand I did in this place at that time. I thank the government for changing its mind once the facts were made known.

I deplore the situation when I see the provinces of Newfoundland and Quebec left alone in respect of the great power resources of the Churchill river which formerly was called the Hamilton river. We should have helped those two provinces. The situation is the same as that in respect of the power on the Nelson river in British Columbia and the Yukon Territory. This government, as a positive dynamic undertaking, should have built a national power grid so that those provinces which own this power could have pumped it east and west before they put in a north and south extension in order to give Canadians first chance at this power on an economic basis and in order to provide greater availability of markets to these provinces or the private companies, whoever owns the power. I do not care whether the resources are owned by a province or by a private company. If it is Canadian, we should back it in a positive, constructive way to get our costs lowered.
As I go through all the various things I want to say here my enthusiasm for Canada rises. Last April Japan made a proposal that Australia, Japan, the United States and Canada join to set common growth rates so that we could meet problems in the same way the common market meets them. There has been no response from either the United States or Canadian governments. These are the failures which depress me. There is so much on the optimistic side, however, that I keep on fighting.
We must have devices in Canada to encourage Canadians on a voluntary basis to take an interest in equity investment. I am not thinking merely of investment at the stabilized stage of industry where we would get 5 per cent on our money. I have in mind the exploration and development stage. This is where the wealth is developed and where the ownership and control are. This is coming, but there is no help from the government. We started a trade promotion drive in 1960. Our exports were $4 billion then. They have risen to $11 billion just because the government gave the leadership. I need not go into the details of that operation, it is well known. I know Canadians have the resources and the know-how. If they have the will, they can do it. If you speak to me in this centennial year about uniting Canadians, I say we can unite Canadians through equality of opportunity and with the knowledge and confidence that we are going to be as wealthy a nation as any industrialized country.
May 16, 1967	COMMONS
Finally, we must make another decision separate from the economic decision involving the three courses I have outlined of continen-talism, restrictive nationalism and expansionist nationalism. I think most of us know where I stand on the economic course. We have, however, another decision which is just as important. I see a trend toward a policy of handouts. I know that 25 per cent of Canadian people live at levels below that which we can tolerate. I know that one and a half billion people around the world live at levels below that which we can tolerate. But there is another way to take action than by handouts. There are programs of self-help. We introduced one when we were the government. It is called ARDA. In this program surveys could be made and knowledge furnished to any group of people who wished that knowledge. Not only would we drain the places which need draining and dam the waters which need damming but we also would get the local people-farmers, businessmen and professional people-working together to raise the income of marginal areas, not just to some miserable level of $3,500 but to a level equal to that of any other family group in the country.
As I travel around world and hear the phrases "ugly Russian" and "ugly American" I know I do not want to hear my country called "ugly Canada". We must promote these self-help programs to give respect to ourselves and those we help. I cannot speak for 100 years ahead, but I hope that in the next century Canadians will back the course of self-help rather than just try to appease their conscience by handouts.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join other hon. members in congratulating the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I thought both hon. members did an excellent job.
In my opinion the most crucial problem besetting parliament today is the need for reform. I know this is a most hackneyed subject and I am almost reluctant to bring it up again. However, I feel that if by repetition we emphasize the importance of this subject our remarks will be justified. We have a grandiose and imaginative program of legislation before us, but there is one point which should be made. We will not be able to enact this legislation quickly and efficiently unless we modernize our parliamentary machinery. What has amazed me since January, 1966 is the amount of legislation we have been able
DEBATES	271
The Address-Mr. Tolmie to enact. This simply means that we could have done more had our procedures been improved. What we have done has been at the expense of long hours and a great toll upon the members of the house.
We have had a spectacular record of achievement. I do not say this in a partisan manner. I believe that all members of the house, even though some may do so grudgingly, give the government credit for its achievements. I say this because if we can eliminate some of the antique procedures which now harass the house we will be able to be much more productive.
What about the future? In the throne speech we are faced with a veritable avalanche of legislation designed to cater to the interests of urban dwellers, interests in the field of domestic relations and in the field of criminal law. I believe this to be good. The veering away from social welfare programs is good. We are now directing our attention to social reform programs. But again there is a catch. If we wish to implement these programs, then not only do we have to tinker and tamper with the machinery of government but to take it apart and reassemble it.
My thesis is very simple. I believe that parliamentary reform should have priority. It should be the bedrock upon which our legislative house is constructed. We have taken a good step in setting up a committee on parliamentary procedure, and I earnestly hope that the committee will undertake its task most seriously. It will delve into the mechanics of parliamentary procedure and into the underlying concept of parliament itself. One might properly ask: If parliamentary procedure is so important then why do we rush so impetuously? The answer is fairly simple. Lurking in the background for years has been a desire for some reform. However, in the past few years, in view of government intervention, social reform and social welfare programs, and problems respecting management and labour relations which confront us, we have needed more legislation. In this very complex society we are besieged by requests for remedial legislation from all types of groups. We have more work, and we are not able to cope with it properly.
There is one very strong factor militating against parliamentary reform and that is the strong clash of opinion as to the role of parliament itself. Some people believe that this chamber should basically be a debating forum. They feel there should be an almost unbridled expression of opinion and that any
May 16, 1967

The Address-Mr. Tolmie step to curtail this will impair the very essence of democracy. This is understandable. I would certainly not want to see any procedures introduced which would in any way stop vigorous and fiery debate or which would make parliament subservient to the whims of the government. However, I believe there is a somewhat pernicious preoccupation with this role of parliament while insufficient attention is paid to the other role of parliament, its duty to transact the country's business. I think we must face the fact that we are running a multibillion dollar business and that we cannot run it with the same rules as we had a hundred years ago. If we are going to translate into action the hopes, aims and aspirations of our people and do it efficiently, we have to change the rules and change them fast.
I make no apology for making certain recommendations. I know they are not original. First of all may I say it is appalling to see new members coming into this chamber without having the slightest grasp of the rules and parliamentary procedure. Most members have no penchant for procedure and no flair for it. They become discouraged and frustrated and thus cannot play a useful role in parliament. On the other hand, there are certain hon. members who have a flair for the rules. In some cases they become very familiar with them but sometimes they use them to their own advantage and to the disadvantage of the house. Therefore I think it would make good sense to train new members. I feel that before any new member takes his seat he should be compelled to listen to lectures for at least one week in which parliamentary procedure, behaviour and ethnics would be explained. I believe this is essential. I also believe we should have a condensed handbook on parliamentary rules. At present we have a large volume but it is difficult to understand and very perplexing. I think such a handbook could be written in the form of questions and answers. It should be available to all members and should contain the highlights of parliamentary procedure.
I believe that sessions should start and end at a specified time. This is necessary for good organization. We will then be able to organize the work of the committees and our own free time, as well as our debates here. But most important of all, we will be able to organize our private lives. Many hon. members realize that our long-suffering wives are harassed by the uncertainties and vicissitudes of politics, and I think it is about time we paid some [Mr. Tolmie.1
attention to this aspect of parliamentary life. If we could organize our leisure time we could make our wives happy. When our wives are happy we are happy and more productive and thus can serve our country better.
I should like to speak now about votes of confidence. I submit that the present situation, if not idiotic, is completely irrational. At present, if the government introduces a bill which is voted down the government falls and we are faced with an election. Such a situation could take place if, for example, 15 or 20 government members were caught in a snowdrift. This is ludicrous. I believe that if the government has to fall this should happen by way of a formal vote of non-confidence at a certain specified time.
If we change this procedure we will eliminate a lot of petty political interplay and petty manoeuvring for advantage. Naturally the opposition would wish to catch the government off guard. So would we if we were in the opposition. But this is something we could do without. No efficient company would allow its directors to be ousted because some shareholders, even a majority of them, disagreed with one facet of their policy. They would only be asked to resign if they lost the confidence of the majority of the shareholders.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Turning to the actual conduct of the house I suggest, in the first place, that there are many things we could improve. For example, we could improve our procedure in connection with ministerial statements. They could be tabled and printed in Hansard. After distribution to the leaders of the opposition parties the debate could then be restricted to five minutes.
I feel that the provision for emergency debates has been much abused. My understanding of the purpose of an emergency debate is to give the opposition an opportunity to bring to the attention of the government something of the utmost national importance which would affect the general welfare of this country. This is not what happens. A member rises in the house fresh from his constituency and presents a local problem. He addresses the house before the assembled press representatives. He makes his point and then he is called the guardian of his constituency. Actually he is wasting the time of the house. Most of these motions are disallowed. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that you should have the privilege of disallowing these motions without debate or that debate be restricted to five
May IB. 1967	COMMONS
minutes with one representative from each party participating.
I believe also that our question period should be completely revamped. I believe in the question period. I think it is essential that the government should be scrutinized and if there are any weaknesses or injustices it is the duty of the opposition to probe deeply. However, I believe this can be done and time saved. What happens now? We have between 20 and 25 well paid executives sitting for an hour a day listening to questions of all types from all sources and without notice. I submit that these gentlemen should be devoting more time to running this country. They should be devoting time to the formulation of policy and to the administration of their departments. This objective could be accomplished if we copied the British system and had certain ministers come into the house for a couple of days a week at scheduled times. They would have notice of the questions to be asked and we would receive better answers. We would have more efficiency.
I believe it is self-evident that we should limit the time spent on debate. All members in this house realize that in most debates we become repetitious and waste time. Most members realize that after a certain length of time a question has been completely aired. They know they are not going to convince anyone to change his mind. They know they are tired and nauseated by the repetition and they know that the country is. I feel that if we cannot allocate time for debates by agreement we should do so by a vote of the house.
I believe speeches should be limited to 20 minutes, Mr. Speaker. In certain cases this time could be extended. I also believe in the principle of filing speeches. This simply means that a person wants to get on the record,-

The Address-Mr. Tolmie moon and can develop I.B.M. machines, then certainly we can introduce a modern voting system.
The committee system has worked very well but it should be improved by better time allocations for sittings and more research staff. My thesis is very simple, Mr. Speaker. I believe that parliamentary reform should have priority over all other legislation. I believe that from it will flow good legislation and efficiency in our operations. Perhaps this should be our parliamentary centennial project.
Why do I say this? May I outline my three reasons for advocating parliamentary reform. Many new members come into this house and become disenchanted, discouraged and disillusioned. They are cast into this mood by the obvious, stupid waste of time. They become disgruntled and discouraged. If we are going to retain members and attract good new members, then we should streamline our procedures. Second, as I said before, if we are going to transact business we have to improve our procedures. At this particular time in our history when we are enacting social legislation to bring about social reforms, we need to be able to proceed quickly. Each day we delay is a day of suffering for those waiting for divorce reform, for those waiting for penal reform, for those waiting for reforms in connection with juvenile delinquency, for those waiting for protection against hate literature, for those desperately needing housing and for those who should be protected against the ravages of pollution. The totality of human suffering and economic waste caused by outdated ritualistic parliamentary procedures staggers the imagination and cries out for help.
Perhaps the most important of all the reasons for a drastic change in our parliamentary procedure is the need to uplift the image of parliament itself. Bluntly and starkly said, rightly or wrongly our parliament is held in low esteem. A vivid picture of endless, futile debates has seeped down to the grass roots of this nation and conjured up an image of bungling, inefficient parliament. We must raise the standards of excellence in parliament so the people of this land will respect this institution and we will thus impart strength and vitality to it. We must increase the prestige of parliament so that parents across this land will be proud tc see their sons adorn this chamber. We must increase the prestige of parliament so that well motivated, well qualified young men in our nation will seek a seat in this venerable house. We cannot do

The Address-Mr. Irvine it by tinkering with the procedures of parliament. We must do it by a drastic and brutal assault on the rules of the house and the basic concepts underlying parliament.
In this our centennial year we are looking for projects, so let us make this our project. In this our centennial year Canadians are told, in flaming, emotional speeches, of the unlimited riches, individual dignity and security awaiting all of us as we enter the second century. Let us provide the means of achieving these most laudable and attainable goals.

speechtext:
It had been my intention in entering this debate to say a few words about our centennial year and the great celebrations we are having throughout the country, and also to say something about our constitution. All these things have been said so many times, and in such an effective way, that I feel perhaps anything I might add would be somewhat redundant. However, to those of others I should like to add my congratulations to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I am sure that this has been a wonderful opportunity for these two new members. Certainly they should be congratulated upon their sincerity of purpose. I do not go along with everything they said, but naturally I would not. At the same time I do want to pass along my congratulations to them.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne might be termed an exercise in futility. I think it conceals a great deal more than it actually reveals. There is an abundance of quantity and an almost complete famine of quality. There is nothing of a very constructive nature. It contains a rehashing of what the government has done, but very little is said about what it intends to do in the future, which I think is so important in this our centennial year. The speech was of extraordinary length and according to one of the editorials I read, had a looseness of
(Mr. Tolmie.]
composition. It was not a reliable forecast of legislation, but an inventory of the desires and dreams of a floundering government.
Some of the items mentioned in the speech are the following: the expansion of designated areas; a job finding program; mobility financing; again the Canada Development Corporation; aid to Indians and Eskimos-all very worthy objectives. There is to be additional foreign aid in the amount, I believe, of $300 million, again a worthy objective. However, perhaps we should think for a little while and ask ourselves whether true charity does not begin at home.
There was no mention of solutions for such things as the staggering national debt that we have at the present time, the terrific burden that is placed upon the taxpayer and the hundreds of thousands of people who are unemployed. The government contend that more people are employed, but this is only natural because there are more people in Canada today. The law of nature sees that we have an increase every year, and people also enter the country as immigrants. Naturally there are more people in Canada today and so more are working; but there are also more unemployed.
Nothing was said, to my knowledge, about what was going to be done to control the spiralling cost of living, or what was going to be done about protecting the man who carries a lunch bucket against the present inflationary economy of this country. What is going to be done about increased government spending year after year, as evidenced by the estimates? The dessert was mentioned, Mr. Speaker, but there was little or no thought given to the main course.
Another matter to which I would draw the attention of the house, and about which I have spoken to the Solicitor General (Mr. Pennell), a man for whom I have the greatest admiration, is that no mention was made in the speech of hate literature and the prohibition of the dissemination of such literature. Last session there were two private members bills on the order paper dealing with this subject. There was Bill No. C-45, to amend, I believe it was, the Post Office Act to forbid the distribution of this type of literature through the mails. Then there was Bill No. C-98, which I believe ws sponsored by the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), having to do with group libel, the dissemination of group hatred. I should have liked to see some reference to this matter in the speech.
May 16, 1967

I have before me a copy of an item which was distributed in my home city of London, as well as in Windsor, Toronto and perhaps other cities. 1 am not going to give the name of the person involved because I am sure that what this individual wants is a little notoriety; but I do not think that this sort of thing is going to contribute very much to the success of this country in our next century. This material is published by a nazi group, so-called, and we surely had enough of them during the second world war and immediately preceding it. It bears the sign of the swastika, and beneath it, at the foot of the page appears the following:
The symbol of the movement which alone can prevent the Star of David from being forced on to us as our flag.
This is hate literature in its worst form, Mr. Speaker. It goes on:
The flag of a mixed racial society must not be forced on us!
Then it goes on to say we should keep our country white and our race pure. This literature is directed at the Jewish people, a people who have made such great contributions to our business, economic and cultural life.
There are those who say, Mr. Speaker, that it is not in the interest of freedom of speech, one of the freedoms which we cherish, to pass legislation prohibiting this kind of thing. However, I contend that a failure to pass legislation forbidding it ignores freedom of religion. We would be picking out one group, then another, and which group would be the next one?
I understand from talking to the Solicitor General that the joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons have been instructed to recommend some kind of legislation to this house in this regard, and that they should do this very soon. I hope that this type of legislation will be presented to us in the immediate future. We have to do something to protect this segment of our society, so let us not hedge or equivocate. These citizens are entitled, the same as any member of this house, to the dignity of the individual. They are also entitled to freedom of religion. I hope that this government does not consider them as second class citizens.
Another subject with which I should like to deal is the maltreatment of children. At the last session I introduced a private members bill, Bill No. C-219, dealing with this very subject, and it was still on the order paper at the end of the session. We have a Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, but we
The Address-Mr. Irvine have no society for the prevention of cruelty to children. How wrong can we be?
The province of Ontario brought in legislation to make it mandatory for people to report any knowledge they had of maltreatment of children, but there were no teeth in that legislation, Mr. Speaker. The bill I introduced last session, and which I intend to reintroduce at this session makes it a criminal offence to fail to report cases of cruelty. It imposes a fine and/or prison term on those working in the medical profession for failing to report cruelty cases and imposes a lesser fine on other individuals. I submit that in the interests of humanity cases of this kind should be reported. Many cases of this sort have come to the attention of hon. members, and many have come to my attention during the four years I have had the privilege of sitting in this chamber.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
One of the most deplorable incidents that happened recently in my riding was where a young couple punished their three and a half year old child for misdemeanours by holding it in boiling water. The child died, and the couple was sentenced to two years imprisonment. That crime was despicable; it was terrible. People who let a child suffer like that ought not to be returned to society until they are psychiatrically sound. They are sick; and there are many like them throughout the country.
Next I want to speak about pension plans for retired civil servants. I wish to quote from a document printed by the public service superannuates. It contains interesting information which I have checked and find to be true, and I wish to put some of it on the record. Our civil servants have served their country well, but are receiving pitiful pensions, although the money is there to increase their pensions; it is their money. I now quote from the document:
The superannuation plan for civil service employees of Canada has been in operation since 1924. The Public Service Superannuation Act contains the authority for its establishment and the provisions for its administration. Section 34 of the P.S.S. Act-
That is the Public Service Superannuation Act:
-requires that the Minister of Finance "shall lay before parliament each year a report on the administration of this act during the preceding fiscal year. . ." Section 32 describes the "amounts to be credited to the account in each fiscal year", and section 35 of the P.S.S. regulations provides how much and when the interest earned on the balance of the account shall be calculated and credited.

May 16, 1967
The Address-Mr. Irvine
According to these annual reports the Minister of Finance shows that the balance at the credit of this account as at March 31, 1965, was $2,161 million-
It has increased since then:
-and that this amount was $304 million higher than the balance at the previous fiscal year end ...
Also, interest alone on the cumulative balance year after year is more than the total annual expenditure. In other words the receipts into the fund are more than three times the expenditures from the fund.
That needs to be looked into carefully. Continuing:
In January of 1966 in answer to questions asked in the House of Commons it was revealed that 5.330 retired civil servants and 6,775 widows of civil servants receive pensions of less than $50.00 a month. Those getting under $100 monthly include 13,109 civil servants and 11,923 widows. It has recently been said by welfare authorities that a couple getting less than $300 a month are living on the fringe of poverty .. .
Coupled with these figures the Dominion Bureau of Statistics tells us that in February the consumer price index rose to a record 142.1 based on the 1949 consumer prices equalling 100. In addition, from the beginning of the war years to the 1949 establishment of this consumer price index, the cost of living rose approximately 60 per cent.
In 25 years the cost of living has doubled, yet the pensions of our retired civil servants have remained the same. Continuing:
The reason why the P.S.S. fund is in the red is because section 3(2) of the P.S.S. Act places the superannuation account in the consolidated revenue fund and the money is thereby used for purposes other than superannuation. The Glassco Commission revealed a shortage in the superannuation account. Moneys collected as contributions toward a pension plan by the administrators or trustees from employer and employee cannot be classified as revenue in the sense that postal, customs, excise, income tax, etc., returns are considered as revenue. Contributions toward the Canada Pension Plan are not being included as revenue. These moneys are being made available for investment.
The provinces are clamouring to use this money at the present time. Continuing:
The Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance have compared the P.S. superannuation plan with outside pension plans, and have said that by granting pension adjustments in favour of federal superannuates they would be discriminating against Canadian citizens. By the way are federal civil servants not Canadian citizens? These gentlemen have omitted to mention that this is a contributory plan ...
In January 1965 employees of the Ford Motor Company of Canada obtained an adjustment in their pensions of $1.45 per month for each year of service. A pensioner with 30 years service thus got a pension increase of $43.50 per month...
Revision of the P.S.S. Act is long overdue. In any revision, consideration should be given to inserting a provision whereby pensions will be adjusted in line with the consumer cost of living

index, as is now being done for the Canada Pension Plan, the Old Age Security, and in the case of salaries and wages paid throughout the civilized world. The British Pensions (Increase) Act has provided pension increases in 1920, 1924, 1944, 1947, 1952, 1954, 1956, 1959, 1962 and 1965 for retired public servants.
It is time that we acted on behalf of our civil servants, many of whom have given dedicated service to this country.
Next I refer to page 590 of Hansard for April 26, 1965 where the following information is found:
The balance of $2,161 million in this account at March 31, 1965 is $304 million higher than the balance at the previous fiscal year end.
This money belongs to our retired civil servants, and we ought to be fair with them. Let us bring their pensions to a decent level.
Next I want to say something about empire building, government by bureaucracy. The figures I shall mention I have researched thoroughly, some of them going back to 1963, when this government took over. It will be interesting to compare these figures with those of today. For instance, in 1963 the C.B.C. had 824 employees; today it has 1,308-almost twice as many. In 1963 the Department of Agriculture employed 10,410; today it employs 12,442. The B.B.G.-much younger and probably much wiser then- employed 40, and today employ 94. The figures for the Department of Fisheries show 2,668 for 1963, and 3,285 employed today. In the Department of Public Works there were 9,290 in 1963 and there are 9,815 today. In the Department of Defence Production-and this is an alarming increase-we had 1,647 in 1963, compared with 5,430 today. The Department of the Secretary of State employed 824 as compared with 1,497 today.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Let us look at the spending estimates of these various departments and see how they have increased since this government took office. Estimates of C.B.C. expenditure have increased by $56 million, which is 70 per cent higher than the 1963 figure. In the ministry of agriculture the increase is $78 million, amounting to 45 per cent. The increase for the Board of Broadcast Governors is $691,000 or 90 per cent. In the Department of Fisheries it is $24 million-a 100 per cent increase. In Public Works it is $98 million or an increase of 55 per cent-I am quoting the nearest round figure below the actual amount in each case.
Mr. Speaker, we cannot afford that kind of government. The estimated expenditure in
May 16, 1967

the fiscal year just ended was $8,795 million. This year it is $9.5 billion-very nearly a billion dollars more. This is at a time when things are pretty good-we hope-and when we should perhaps be laying something aside for a day when it might be needed. Somebody has to pay the piper, and it is the taxpayer. It is the man in the income bracket between $5,000 and $10,000 who pays most of the income tax which is collected in Canada.
The present administration is spending money like a drunken sailor. This is an expensive government and the taxpayer just cannot afford it. If we consider this picture of taxation and expenditure together with the disunity which seems to be running through the cabinet at the present time it may be concluded that this is a good time for the government to resign. Let them resign now. Let us get ourselves a government which would protect the individual, the average person, so that he can live in at least a semblance of dignity.
Today the average person pays 34 cents out of every dollar he makes in taxes of one form or another. I contend that the burden of taxation has reached the point at which he can stand no more. Consider the increases which have taken place in the field of wages-increases which amount to about 10 per cent a year. Compare this rate of increase with the rate of increase of our productivity. Last year national productivity was supposed to have increased by 6 per cent but the influence of factors such as price indexes brought the net increase down to about 4-J per cent.
If wages are increasing at twice the rate of the increase in our productivity, something has to be done. If not, we shall price ourselves completely out of foreign markets-and when we do that we shall really be in trouble, because once we lose those markets we shall find ourselves facing mass unemployment, something we cannot afford with prices as high as they are at present.
I suggest to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson), who I see in the house now, that the government should take a good look at this situation. I am seriously concerned as to the direction in which we are going, and I know he is, too. What is the answer? In my own minimal way I have a few thoughts on the subject:
1.	We should bring about a gigantic cut in all expenditures. Let us cut and trim everything as closely as we can. Anyone who operates a business, whether big or small, public or corporate, knows that if the money going
The Address-Mr. Ryan out is more than the money coming in, something has to be done about it. This is the position in which we find ourselves today.
2.	We must increase our productivity by every means open to us.
3.	We must get back to common sense business principles-we cannot pay out more than we receive.
4.	We must return to the old fashioned, outmoded method of pay as you go, which is still, to my way of thinking, the ideal way. Why not a balanced budget for a change? The Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) will shortly be presenting a budget to us. I hope that somehow he will be able to present us with at least a balanced budget; we would like to think that in this our centennial year we are heading in the right direction. We should be looking forward and upward-and when I say "upward" I do not mean that our expenditures should be going in this direction. It is time for each of us in all parties in this house to get together and put our country first, and petty party grievances second.
