speechtext:
I should like to begin by complimenting the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I believe all hon. members will agree with me when I say the house has two new found stars, one from Newfoundland and the other from Quebec. They are to be commended on the excellent manner in which they carried out their assignments.
As chairman of our Canadian NATO parliamentary association I feel I should take the opportunity afforded by this debate to speak for my allotted time with respect to certain aspects of foreign affairs which are dealt with in the speech from the throne. On the premise that our constant objective is to strengthen Canada's position in the councils of nations by the ardent pursuit of world peace, I believe we must, with strength, face up to current international problems.
We fear the proliferation of nuclear arms and are dismayed at the slow progress being made in the field of international disarmament. We recognize the urgent need for the reform of the NATO alliance and acknowledge that our NORAD arrangements require adjustment. The alternate periods of cold war and detente between east and west greatly complicate these problems.
As my time is limited, I intend to confine myself to speaking about the reform of NATO and the North Atlantic Assembly. I shall try to deal with these subjects as I see them, as chairman of our local NATO association and

May 16, 1967
The Address-Mr. Ryan as your representative on the standing committee of the North Atlantic Assembly. With respect to the reform of NATO, I shall endeavour to give hon. members some background on the origin of NATO, some details of Canada's present contribution to NATO, and the original and current Canadian view of it as compared with the American view. Then I shall deal with current problems and the need for reform.
During the second world war, Russia annexed Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, certain parts of Finland, Poland, Rumania, northeast Germany and eastern Czechoslovakia. She took over 180,000 square miles of territory and more than 23 million inhabitants. After the war, by 1948, Moscow controlled and swallowed another 363 million square miles of territory and 95 million people. Her pressure extended menacingly into various other parts of the world, ranging from Greece in the Balkans to Korea in Asia. The west was scared into action.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
Free Europe turned to the United States, the only power strong enough to withstand the might of the U.S.S.R. On March 12, 1947, President Truman enunciated the Truman doctrine. Congress responded with $400 million in aid and dispatched military and civilian missions to Greece and Turkey. The Marshall plan extended aid to all Europe, including Russia and her satellites behind the iron curtain, but no Soviet state or satellite was permitted to accept this aid, and the conditions between east and west became what is described as the cold war.
On March 17,	1948, Belgium, France,
Luxemburg, The Netherlands and the United Kingdom signed the Brussels Treaty which pledged mutual co-operation in building up a common defence system and the strengthening of economic and cultural aids. Three months later the Russians countered with the blockade of Berlin. Canada welcomed the Brussels Treaty, and promised to support an effective system of collective security through regional pacts under the charter of the United Nations. The Canadian suggestion for a mutual defence alliance received support in Britain and in the United States. After a series of talks between representatives of Canada, the United States and those of the Brussels treaty powers, the text of the treaty was published on March 18, 1949. Denmark, Iceland, Italy, Norway and Portugal were officially invited to accede to the treaty, and on April 4, 1949, in spite of official protests

from the Soviet union, the North Atlantic Treaty was signed in Washington by the foreign ministers of 12 countries, including Canada, and the parliaments of all countries ratified the treaty within five months thereafter. Greece and Turkey were invited to join and formally acceded on February 18, 1952. The Federal Republic of Germany officially became a member on May 9, 1955, to bring the membership of the alliance to 15 countries.
Canada's contribution to NATO defence is a combination of land, sea and air elements of its armed forces. In West Germany, in the Soest area, we have stationed the 4th Canadian Infantry Brigade, consisting of approximately 6,300 officers and men under Brigadier Amy. This force is kept at a high state of readiness, at a cost of about $54 million annually, excluding weapons. The Canadian government is in the process of re-equipping the brigade with new and modern vehicles and weapons.
Our delegation to the NATO Parliamentarians Conference held in Paris last November had the privilege, before the conference, of visiting the 4th brigade at Soest and can attest to its superlative condition and spirit. The delegation also inspected two of our four air bases in France and Germany. At Marville, France, we saw the highly efficient CF-104 reconnaissance operations that are carried out by No. 1 wing of the air division. Later the group proceeded with Air Vice Marshal Lane to No. 4 wing at Baden Soel-lingen in Germany where we toured the facilities and were briefed as far as possible on the state of readiness of our modern aircraft. The high degree of professionalism possessed by our military officers and men was quite apparent, and we were very proud of them.
In addition we have other troops that are committed to NATO but are maintained in Canada. Also maintained in Canada is a special force, a 3,176 man battalion group for the ACE Mobile Force. ACE is under the Supreme Allied Commander Europe, SACEUR, and is designed for quick action to meet any aggression on the NATO flanks, such as in Norway, Greece or Turkey, or to meet any other similar contingency. The present commander of ACE is a Canadian, General Turcot. Last summer Canada offered NATO two more battalions for ACE Mobile Force and recently the offer was accepted in principle.
May 16, 1967

One of the most important roles that Canada played in the founding of the North Atlantic Alliance was to bring the United States into the treaty. However, from the outset there have continued to be basic differences in the views, aims and attitudes of the Canadian and American governments. Even today, while they both generally consider NATO to be indispensable, yet in need of change from its present form, they have come to these conclusions by different ways and for different reasons. Thus they tend to different solutions of the basic problems that are facing NATO.
Canada has always, from the beginning looked on the alliance as the basis of a future Atlantic community. Beyond the military tasks Canadians saw the ultimately more important political, economic, social and agricultural roles. She tried to incorporate specific proposals along these lines in the treaty itself, but failed because the larger powers were not too enthusiastic. The best that was achieved was the insertion of Article II in the treaty, that is the article which contains the nonmilitary provisions.
During the Truman-Eisenhower days the United States viewed NATO as a purely military association, with the one task of defending Europe, a policy with which Canada has never entirely agreed. The Canadian outlook has at no time considered NATO in its actual form as a solely military alliance for the defence of Europe. We have sought for greater unities, but despite disagreement as to the ultimate aims of the alliance Canada has supported moves toward the integration of the armed forces of NATO members, and opposed demands for exceptions.
Hopes were high at one time of NATO transforming itself into a close association of free countries on both sides of the Atlantic, but again the larger powers have not encouraged the extension of it into other fields. The United States Congress, for example, has continued to be opposed to any form of foreign control of United States policy.
As a defence alliance NATO has proven to be a tremendous success. Its existence has diminished the danger to western Europe, and that very fact has raised problems within the alliance. By 1958 the British were critical of the fact that NATO had failed to work out a common policy on a global basis, and France was not satisfied with preponderant American influence in NATO. President de Gaulle sought a permanent directorate composed of the representatives of the United States,
The Address-Mr. Ryan Britain and France to co-operate their policies the world over. The American response to this was chilling, and apart from the big three it was already clear that the other members of the alliance, including Canada, sought more consultation and less domination under the guise of co-ordination.
In addition to the political and economic problems of the alliance, the late President Kennedy had to come to grips with the question of control over nuclear weapons. He evolved a formula in 1962 which indicated that the United States would be ready to share a nuclear weapon partnership with a United States of Europe, but with the diminishing danger to western Europe it proved impossible to take even a first step in the direction of a united Europe.
Many Canadians, of course, did not like the idea of a dualist NATO, or a two-pillar policy, one pillar being in Europe and the other being in North America. This type of partnership would be entirely counter to our traditional foreign policy. What has been important to Canada is that her association be on an equal footing with all NATO countries, as only this structure gives Canada a degree of independence from the United States, a degree of independence that we have considered in the past to be essential.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Another Canadian consideration is that a two-pillar partnership would put Canada in the agonizing position of having to make a choice between opposing American and European policies, on frequent occasions. But the natural trends on both sides of the Atlantic are toward continentalism. Con-tinentalism is a process in operation today that is analogous to the process that brought about confederation in this country 100 years ago.
Canada does not seem to have changed her attitude with regard to President Kennedy's dualist NATO proposal, although circumstances in Europe may very well eventually dictate such a situation-at least with regard to the military aspect of the alliance. Britain's entry into the common market is an example. Will a United States of Europe follow? Will we be forced to change our attitude to remain in the alliance? We are going to need strong leadership and strong support in Canada to keep our independence in our second century.
The nuclear dilemma was not a problem during the early years of the alliance when the concept of the defence of Europe coincided with the concept of the defence of

May 16, 1967
The Address-Mr. Ryan America, and when all the partners in the alliance felt that an assault upon any one of the members would immediately bring forward massive retaliation. By 1959 however the strategic situation had changed. There was talk of a missile gap in favour of the Soviet union, which made Europeans doubt that the American guarantee was unequivocal, and would be instantaneously operative as had been believed earlier.
Then President Kennedy evolved the new look in American strategic thinking, based on the correlated ideas of flexible or measured response and strict central control. The intent was to avoid the necessity to meet every one of the enemies choices with the massive retaliation of the earlier era. The United States now wanted a range of options and the right to discharge its commitments in NATO according to the circumstances, with conventional arms at first and as long as possible, and with nuclear arms if necessary, but in that case with the discretion assured by the tightest and most responsible central control.
This de facto change has had an unsettling effect upon the European side of the alliance, as it did not meet European security requirements or European aspirations. However, today most Europeans are less troubled, now that they have witnessed the American response to the Cuban crisis and have been shown the plans for flexible and measured response. However, a continuing trouble with the policy of flexible response under central control is that it is inconsistent with the political concept of a two-pillar partnership; the latter policy envisages a united Europe with which the United States would share the control of nuclear weapons, and also the west's responsibility for peace, stability and prosperity in the world.
The idea of central control, on the other hand, is based on the idea of integration under United States direction. This apparent contradiction strengthens the European suspicion that the United States really wants acceptance of its military program and only holds out the additional promise of a true partnership in front of the allies to get them to accept such an arrangement.
So today the problems of consultation and the proliferation of nuclear weapons in NATO are two that are still to be solved satisfactorily. Mutual control may well be deferred until Europe achieves political status equal to the United States. In the meantime, it appears that the furthest the United States is willing to go is to allow participation in the formulation of a plan of priorities that will come into

operation in the event of an emergency. Mutual control continues to be, therefore, the major problem facing NATO today-although the West German desire for a greater role in the determination of alliance policy, and for a more tangible voice in nuclear weapon sharing has been met in part by the recent setting up of the nuclear planning committee.
Another key problem facing NATO today arises by virtue of the effects of French policies on alliance cohesion. Since 1962, the shape and purpose of NATO have come under increasing attack by France. Under the leadership of President de Gaulle, France makes three specific arguments.
The nuclear balance of power between the Soviet union and the United States has seriously impaired the credibility of the United States deterrent. France believes that it is unlikely the United States will risk its own survival in order to counter a Soviet attack in Europe, or that the Soviet union will doubt the will of the United States in a European showdown. In this respect France does not trust the United States; but other members of the alliance, including Canada, continue to do so.
Because of the strategic stalemate in Europe, the French believe that the real area of conflict between east and west has shifted from Europe to the former colonial territories. The French fear that unless they, and the other European states, remain aloof from these extra-European struggles, they may become involved in a war that is neither to their interest, nor of their own making.
Because a nuclear stalemate does exist, and because the main theatre of concentration is no longer in Europe, the French believe that there is no longer any need to maintain the NATO military structure. Indeed the French believe that this organization is merely a means of subordination. The organization, in President de Gaulle's view, is a method by which the United States maintains its domination of NATO.
By withdrawal from the military infrastructure of NATO, France has not broken the letter of the North Atlantic Treaty. This is apparent from a careful reading of the articles of the treaty. Whether it has, however, broken the spirit of the treaty, or any bilateral agreement in respect of the infrastructure, is another matter.
The French still want to be a partner in NATO politically, and in the event of an emergency, militarily, under French sovereignty. Furthermore they want partnership
May 16. 1967

in NADGE-the electronic curtain that will identify all aircraft crossing NATO borders and automatically institute action previously decided upon. The French withdrawal has embarassed the remaining 14 members. Their withdrawal has created many problems for the alliance, many of which have now been solved as the remaining partners have stood steadfastly together, bearing in mind that there are still 300,000 Russian soldiers in East Germany, and that there are six or seven hundred nuclear armed missiles aimed at western Europe.
The German problem is a key problem, both within NATO and between NATO and the Soviet union. After 22 years, the scars of war are not healed and Germany is still a divided nation. Berlin, the capital of a once united Germany, is still in the middle of communist East Germany. There has been no peace settlement; barbed wire and walls separate the east and west Germans. These conditions are highly volatile, and Europe will not rest until they no longer exist. And within the alliance West Germany is seeking to strengthen its political voice through greater influence on military strategic affairs.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
From all this it will be seen that Europe is no longer a downtrodden and helpless continent. The new Europe is now demanding political power commensurate with its potential military and actual economic strength. The United States having long striven toward exactly this situation of European strength, now finds itself somewhat uncomfortable. For the first time there is a challenge to Washington's leadership.
To the French, nuclear subordination seems to imply political subordination. It means that without an independent nuclear force there can be no independent European diplomacy. Even President de Gaulle admits that while his strategic force will have limited military effectiveness, there is every likelihood that it will carry diplomatic weight out of proportion to its size.
Another problem for NATO is the current globalization debate. The United States would like its NATO partners to recognize that it is in their international interests to take a more active role in conflicts and problems outside the Atlantic area, such as Viet Nam. Some other partners are interested in those areas, such as Africa, where they have special relations, but most of the NATO members are reluctant to have any part of globalization. The United States may be able to interest
The Address-Mr. Ryan some of its partners on a bilateral basis but it is fairly apparent that it will not be able to do so on a NATO basis.
When the 12th NATO Parliamentarians Conference was held at NATO political headquarters in Paris last November, two main events occurred; first, the name of the organization was changed to North Atlantic Assembly and, second, a Canadian, our colleague Jean-Eudes Dube, the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska, was elected first president under its new name. Among the many reports, resolutions and recommendations of the conference was one dealing with institutionalization or, if you will, consultative assembly status for the conference, under its new name. This was the second resolution of the political committee and it was adopted by the plenary session of the conference.
It is the hope of the North Atlantic Assembly that it will attain the status of a consultative assembly such as the consultative assembly of the council of Europe, and the European parliament; that it will have more status and influence and be of more assistance to the North Atlantic Council.
The consultative assembly of the council of Europe meets for about a month each year, usually divided into three sessions. It is estimated that an Atlantic assembly would need to meet each year for at least a week. The seat of the assembly would be at the headquarters of NATO in Belgium. It is suggested that the number of its members be 172 of whom 12 would be from Canada. Each member, or substitute, would have one vote and would speak and vote on his own responsibility. The assembly would debate issues currently before the North Atlantic Council for resolution, and would submit new proposals or recommendations. It would submit questions to the Secretary General of the North Atlantic Council and receive either answers or formal refusals to answer. It would invite representatives of the Secretary General or the North Atlantic Council to appear before the assembly or its committees, to question them orally. Such functions are among those possessed by existing European assemblies.
There would appear to be general enthusiasm in favour of the resolution by all member nations, save that certain difficulties may arise when it comes to obtaining ratification for the new status from the parliaments of all countries.
Our own Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) has already indicated
May 16, 1967

The Address-Mr. Cantelon
that the Canadian government favours increasing the importance of the NATO parliamentarians. He has qualified his approval of the proposal to change the NATO Parliamentarians Conference into a consultative assembly by saying, however, that it has not been decided whether the specific proposal adopted by the NATO Parliamentarians Conference represents the best means of giving effect to this objective.
The NATO Parliamentarians Conference now known as the North Atlantic Assembly, has its own secretariat and it is anticipated that this secretariat will be strengthened this year by the appointment of a new Secretary General and an assistant, in addition to the existing staff.
The debates and recommendations of the NATO parliamentarians have been quite influential in moving NATO from peace keeping to peace making, and from conduct of the cold war to a serious interest in the development of the current European detente. NATO parliamentarians are very much interested in exploring and exploiting a rapprochement between east and west, in the interests of a peaceful and lasting settlement in Europe. Increased stature granted by the award of consultative assembly status would likely improve east-west relations because it would be greatly concerned with them and may be the first basic step toward ultimate Atlantic union. Indeed it is possible that its establishment might lead in the future to a reduction in the number of international parliamentary bodies through a merging of the assembly and the assembly of Western European Union. Since the Western European Union is composed of seven NATO countries, such a merger could come about if it appeared to be in the interest of their governments. In this case the specialized functions of the Western European Union assembly could be performed within the framework of an Atlantic assembly, by the delegates from the seven Western European Union members.
In conclusion, I would ask that all hon. members of this house and the other place support the proposal to institutionalize the North Atlantic Assembly, in such fashion as you may be called upon to do so by our government.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I should like to ally myself with those who have congratulated the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne for the very able

manner in which they have discharged their responsibilities. Many have said that seldom have more efficient and capable speeches been delivered. I agree, although my experience here has been rather limited in that regard.
I do not feel I would like to make any general comments on the speech from the throne, because were I to do so I would be compelled to do what many other members have done; that is, suggest that it is so diffuse and so indefinite that it is very difficult actually to make any concrete suggestions about it. I should like to say also that, as this is our centennial year, I am happy that the centennial commission has done such a good job. In particular I should like to mention the name of the commissioner, but perhaps I should not mention his name because everybody knows who he is. I believe he has done an excellent job, although there have been occasions when he seems to have been pushed somewhat into the background. Nevertheless I am sure the work he has done will be recognized by the Canadian people.
I am happy also that in this centennial year our Expo shows evidence of being a great success. I have been very fortunate in having been there on several occasions. I can say, I am sure without fear of contradiction, that all those who visit Expo will enjoy their visit very much. If they wish to receive an education, they can remain there for a couple of weeks and have a rather broad general education in respect of all that is going on in this world today. In particular I think this is noticeable in the pavilions of what I might call the main powers. I refer to the Russian pavilion, the United States pavilion, the British and French pavilions. Since I am a western Canadian I should not like to let this opportunity pass without mentioning that the western Canadian pavilion I visited was I believe the most imaginative and interesting that one could see.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
In considering what I wanted to say today I thought I would like to deal with three topics. The first one is of course my own particular fetish. I suppose this is natural, since I am a schoolteacher. I should like to speak briefly about education and the place of the federal government in that field, because I am not one who believes that the federal government should play no part in education. In a modem and developed nation, such as we are, we should recognize the absolute necessity of a well educated population. We are lagging in this respect.
May 16, 1967

It has been said that in the 20 years after the first war we made very rapid strides, and this applies in particular to the province of Ontario. Since that time I do not think we have kept pace with the developments that have been going on in other countries. Certainly we have not kept pace in the numbers we are educating. The last figures I saw, and I will admit they are a couple of years out of date, showed that some 70 per cent of the Russian people go on to advanced education, that is university or its equivalent. In the United States some 33 per cent continue their education above the high school level, but in Canada only 17 per cent do so.
I know that some years ago we in Canada suffered under the delusion that we had one of the best educational systems in the world. I think it is one of the best for the people who get it, but the trouble is there are not enough people who get it and there will not be enough people getting it until the federal government gives substantial assistance to the provinces in a fund raising manner. One might say that this would be interfering with the prerogatives of the provinces. However, we manage to give educational assistance to the universities without interfering with the special educational prerogatives of the provinces. We manage to give vocational assistance and to pay the largest portion of the capital costs of vocational buildings. Unfortunately the present government has taken a very retrograde step in having removed this provision.
I think we could give that assistance to high schools in the same way. There is no earthly reason why the provinces cannot say to the federal government: we have a certain number of schools we wish to build, and we will require certain sums of money for that purpose. The federal government should be prepared to provide that money to the provinces. If to anyone here this seems too altruistic or too much in opposition to the B.N.A. Act then I do not think he is a modern Canadian and I do not think he really appreciates the difficulties which face education today. I do not think he realizes that unless we do this sort of thing this country in the future will not be able to maintain its position at the forefront of the world's industry, but will lag further and further back. I have some grandchildren in Canada. I hate to think that in the future they might find that this country has lost its place in the parade of nations because it has failed to do for education what obviously needs to be done.

The Address

Mr. Cantelon
The second subject about which I wanted to speak briefly is that of chemical tariffs. It can be only a few words because new developments are taking place in this particular field and I hesitate to comment on this topic in any depth until I have had an opportunity to review the recent work, in particular the publication that came out today. I want to speak about chemical tariffs and what needs to be done for the chemical industry in this country. This is a subject which I as a Sas-katchewanite hold dear to my heart. I believe that Saskatchewan has the industrial base to become the centre of a great new chemical industry in this country. The largest known potash deposit in the world is to be found in Saskatchewan. There are huge deposits of low-grade lignite coal in the south. There will be an adequate supply of water, once we get the South Saskatchewan river dam properly working. There is much oil in my province, and there will be more, I am sure.
I think these three things alone are enough to provide a base for a tremendous development in industrial chemicals. However, there are difficulties here. Until the present time the chemical industry has had to be supported by tariffs, and these tariffs are in the process of revision. As I have said I hesitate to comment on this topic at the present time. Nevertheless I do think we should remember that if we are going to develop an industry in this country, we will have to continue to give it protection. We are a comparatively small country and our production will be small for many years. Therefore we cannot compete with the huge industries that are located in countries like the United States, which is so close to us and so easily able to ship to us the chemicals we want. I think this is probably all that I will say about that particular topic today, although I hope to say more about it some time in the future.
The third subject I want to discuss is that of pollution. So far it has not been too serious in western Canada, but I can foresee a future in which it will be a very serious problem. Generally speaking, there are of course two main classes of pollution with which we as a nation have to deal. The first is air pollution which is caused by two main sources, industrial plants and automobiles. In the west, automobiles do not cause much trouble because there are miles and miles of roads and not too many motorcars to run on them. To those members who like driving a car I would
May 16, 1967

The Address-Mr. Cantelon
suggest a trip to the west because I can assure them they will enjoy it there, tar more than driving on the streets of Ottawa.
I will dismiss rather unwillingly the latter form of pollution by saying that this government, in spite of the lead given it by the United States government and by the vigorous representations made by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey), has made it very clear that it intends to continue its standard policy of moving only when forced to do so. It would be so easy to start now, but of course it will not, as it has told us over and over again.
Fortunately for most of us, industrial air pollution is almost invariably accompanied by such a disagreeable smell that public outcries usually bring some measure of treatment. Nevertheless, both the municipal and provincial governments are very loath to act before the industrial pollution begins. They want the business to come into the province so will not propose the restraint before the industry locates there.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
In Saskatchewan large quantities of salt waste produced as a by-product of the potash industry are almost certain to be blown over many square miles of good farmland. This is a new type of pollution, and there is of course no actual measure to control it at present. I hope that before this pollution becomes very harmful there will be steps taken to prevent the areas around these potash mines from being turned into agricultural deserts.
It is true, of course, that some research is being done. As James H. Gray put it in the Ottawa Citizen for January 23, 1967:
Research is now being done on the effects of airborne salt dust on soils and agricultural crops.
The federal government, I think, would do well to assist in this research as it ought to do in all industrial airborne pollution. I would hope that it would not adopt the attitude of the manager of the Saskatchewan Power Corporation who was quoted as saying:
Water is for use and if some of it gets polluted in the process, the people should try to live with it.
I cannot imagine a more iniquitous type of statement. I cannot imagine, either, the previous manager making that kind of statement. Since the present manager is an appointee of the Liberal government of Saskatchewan, he evidently mirrors the opinion of that government. I hope the premier of Saskatchewan does not feel that way. If he does, I hope he does not delay too long in calling an election

so the people of Saskatchewan can get rid of him and put in a party with more concern for the welfare of the people of my province.
A great deal of attention has been focused on pollution of the Great Lakes watershed. The United States is fortunate in that some ten states are concerned. The federal government there has therefore seen pollution as a national question and has taken an active interest in the problem. As the Winnipeg Free Press put it in an article on April 18, 1966:
The U.S. government appears to be moving in to grasp control firmly on its side of the border, using a combination of legislation, knuckle rapping, potential court actions and money.
It is just too bad our federal government has not the same sort of courage. In 1966 President Johnson proposed to spend $20 million on pollution control research and as much as $10 billion in the next ten years. He estimates it will take $30 billion to clean up water pollution in the United States. I hope we never get to the stage where it will take $30 billion to solve this problem; but if we go on doing nothing, as we have in the past, then we can expect it will cost that amount some day.
Is it that we do nothing because we are afraid to interfere with provincial rights? I believe that is the excuse the government uses today. This is the excuse the government uses to do nothing in spite of the great damages that failure to act has done and continues to do to the national heritage of the people. Dr. Vance of the Ontario Water Resources Commission says:
They're Ontario waters but they're also national waters. As far as I know, it isn't a case of disputed jurisdiction, but clarification is needed.
The Canadian government has evaded its responsibilities long enough. I hope a bold enough step will be taken to do some good. I cite this situation to illustrate the fact that where pollution is worst the government has taken no steps. As the Ottawa Citizen of February 14, 1966 put it in reporting the words of George Burt, Canadian director of the united auto workers at a water conference:
Mr. Pearson's office backs on the Ottawa river which is full of pollution .. . Just across from his office, the E. B. Eddy Company every day dumps tons of sulphur, which I understand is a fish killer, into the river.
Referring to the minister for external affairs he said:
I don't think Paul Martin should be hesitant in making a statement either. He lives on an open sewer-the Detroit river.
May 16. 1967	COMMONS DEBATES	285
The Address-Mr. Cantelon
So we have, as the headlines put it, "politicians living by open sewers", and doing nothing about it. The government certainly has done nothing concrete in the rest of Canada.
In the fall of 1966 there was a conference held on pollution which produced 15 pages of recommendations. I should like to review them briefly, and will condense the recommendations by lumping them under six headings.
First, they decided there was a great need for a federal organization or agency which would develop a pollution abatement code and co-ordinate and disseminate any available information. This organization, too, would conduct research and co-operate with other agencies that might be working in the field. It was also their considered opinion that there should be some form of national standard set up in the pollution field.
Third, they believed that anyone who pollutes should bear the cost of treatment of the pollution damage which is inflicted on other people by the failure to control the pollution. Fourth, the conference considered there ought to be financial incentives to industry so that industry would improve its anti-pollution measures.
Fifth, they noted that there was a shortage of trained experts in the field of pollution. Finally, they thought that the best way to attack pollution control was to do it on a regional or water-shed basis, and to attack it on a multifunctional basis. There were some 600 experts at this meeting and these recommendations were the consensus of their views. This being so, I hope this government, which has never been too willing to accept suggestions, and certainly not too prompt to carry them out, will move rapidly to implement the suggestions that have been made. It is now more than six months since this pollution control group met and brought out these recommendations. I hope it will not be six months before we hear of them again from the government.
Two Ottawa scientists recently presented a paper on the subject of pollution to the Canadian Operational Research Council which was meeting at the University of Ottawa. Dr. R. W. Durie and Dr. R. F. Fletcher of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources presented this paper last Wednesday, May 10. Dr. Durie offers this broad definition of pollution, that it is any effect resulting from the use of natural resources which is deleterious
to man, to his use of natural resources or to his esthetic sense.
In his view, the tendency now is to concentrate on individual problems instead of finding out the best way of using all natural resources. He thinks that we must make an immediate attack on the pollution that exists. He would set up some demonstration projects to show the public what alternatives are available in any plans for pollution control. He believed that the matter of pollution control requires top to bottom planning, because the broad goals must first be set out. I am not too sure what he means by top to bottom planning, but if I were to interpret it I would say it means from the federal government down to the municipal government, as well as the industry or individual which does the polluting.
In the west, and particularly in my own province of Saskatchewan, a study of the industrial pollution of rivers has recently been undertaken. Recently in Saskatchewan an organization was set up by the provincial government to review the matter of pollution. In my own constituency of Kindersley, and also in The Battlefords, this matter of pollution is one that has aroused some interest in the past and is still arousing a good deal of interest because the Saskatchewan river goes through our constituencies.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
The city of Saskatoon has been turning its sewage into the South Saskatchewan river for a great many years. The municipality of Cory which surrounds the city has obtained an injunction to prevent this; but in sp'te of this the city has gone on pollut ng the river. The main argument of the city of Saskatoon today is that it cannot afford present requirements for pollution control unless more aid is forthcoming from the senior levels of government.
This, in effect, was the basis of a brief which was presented to the Saskatchewan Water Resources Commission by the utilities manager for the city. I will not debate the arguments pro and con between this gentleman and the members of the committee. Suffice it to say that there was some conflict of interest between the two and the city was accused of not doing anything. I quote from the Saskatoon Star Phoenix of May 1, 1967:
The brief said pollution programs can cost individuals and organizations large amounts of money with no direct benefit. However, this should not relieve them of the responsibility of protecting a natural resource.
May 16, 1967

The Address-Mr. Cantelon
Since many urban centres are encumbered to the limit with other heavy costs of rapid growth, further extensive costs for pollution control cannot be met from the present available sources of capital and revenue, it said.
Further on it says:
The city felt financial aid offered by the federal government to finance the cost of trunk collector sewers and sewage treatment facilities is inadequate.
The city of Saskatoon's main contention was that it needs more help and, in particular, needs help from the federal government. This is the common complaint of municipalities today.
The North Saskatchewan river runs through the cities of North Battleford and Prince Albert. The city of North Battleford presented a brief to this same committee of the Saskatchewan government in which it said that some provinces tend to claim sole rights to water flowing in any river within their boundaries, and that they claim the right to use and dispose of this resource as they see fit without regard to people who are living outside the provincial boundary. Of course, it is quite evident that this type of thinking is wrong, because a river does not stop at a boundary, either toward its mouth or toward its source. Therefore something should be done to change this sort of provincial attitude.
To my mind it is the sort of thing that demands legislation and action by the federal government in order to prevent those places that are down river from being bothered by pollution from cities that are in other jurisdictions than their own. Certainly it emphasizes the need for national control.
The city of North Battleford has had a good deal of trouble with pollution of the North Saskatchewan river, and has had very little satisfaction in its attempts to try to correct this pollution. Until measures are taken by the federal government in conjunction with the provincial governments to prevent pollution of this type, I doubt very much that anything satisfactory will come of the city's attempts.
The development of effective pollution controls in Saskatchewan cannot be successful unless there is agreement between the province of Saskatchewan and the province of Alberta. And of course, since Manitoba is down river, they have the same right to satisfactory agreements. Since this is so, it seems to me that there is very little possibility of

any satisfactory arrangement unless the federal government can step in and arrange controls that will satisfy all provinces. I think it is particularly important that the federal government should assist, because as the Star Phoenix of May 4, 1967 points out:
Municipal governments across the land are feeling the strain of demands upon property taxes. The problem is particularly acute in cities like Saskatoon where services must be supplied for many residents whose employers pay taxes to other municipal governments.
Further on it says:
We believe that those primarily responsible for causing pollution should also be primarily responsible for the cost of reducing or eliminating that pollution. But some assistance in these matters from provincial and federal governments can be justified.
Then it goes on to say:
The province should have a clear policy on such assistance before it starts to enforce rigid pollution controls-as it hopes to do this summer.
But it is perfectly clear from this, to my mind, that the province cannot have a clear policy on assistance or on rigid pollution controls until it knows just where it stands with the federal government on these matters.
Before concluding this particular portion of my remarks I would like to say a few words about what is going to happen to the South Saskatchewan river dam if something is not done to control pollution in the South Saskatchewan river. Just last summer one of the residents of Saskatoon, Mr. Hugh Arscott, with his son made a trip down the South Saskatchewan river. He came to the conclusion that lake Saskatchewan behind the South Saskatchewan river dam would slowly fill up, without adequate protection from upstream pollution. In his words, "It could very easily become the cesspool of the prairies". He told of a situation near Estuary at the junction of the Red Deer and Saskatchewan rivers where there were brownish-orange suds forming on the river surface, and again, to use his own words, "I cannot tell you what it was, for my fear of disease was greater than my scientific curiosity and no samples were taken for analysis".
In the Red Deer river, which is a tributary to the South Saskatchewan, he noted a chemical factory spewing large quantities of industrial waste into the river. It resulted in a thick brown scum which formed on his boat cover and on the gravel of the river bed. In his own words again, "It doesn't take any talent to pollute a waterway; it's easy". This seems all too true.
May 16, 1967

It will be a shame il the large lake behind the South Saskatchewan river dam does become polluted, for the people of Saskatchewan hope that it will not only be an assistance to industrial development in their province through the power generated at the dam and through the irrigation water they can take from the lake, but that it will also provide a large summer resort area in which all types of water sports can take place. I am sure they hope that it does not become a second lake Erie.
I am not sure whether my time has nearly run out, Mr. Speaker. If not, I should like to call it six o'clock.

I should like to thank hon. members and I assure them I will take only a minute or two.
I wish to close my remarks by making a few comments upon a situation which ought to concern all Canadians. It ought to concern them because we all want to take pride in our* national capital. Across the river from our:

288	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Cantelon parliament buildings lies the plant of the E. B. Eddy Company. It is a modern plant and it is becoming more so as its operations are updated. No one will deny that the company has made laudable attempts to beautify its area, but it is certain that these efforts will result in only limited success. Piles of logs and industrial buildings cannot be turned into things of beauty.
There is only one solution as far as I can see, and that is to move the plant. This is not impossible though it would be expensive. I believe we ought to accept such an expense if we consider that this nation of ours has a future. The immediate question is: what will it cost? My inquiries have obtained the following answers. The plant is worth about $40 million and the 80 acres on which it is situated are assessed at approxiamtely $250 million.
Let us say, then, that the relocation of the plant might today cost the Canadian people about $300 million. If we leave the plant where it is until some time in the future when, I am certain, we shall decide that it must be moved, it would cost a great deal more to do so than it would cost today, besides leaving us for many years with what I was about to call an unsightly sight-perhaps that expression is a little too Irish, but I shall use it anyway-across the river from our beautiful parliament buildings.
We ought to move it, and we ought to do so before the area becomes so crowded and so valuable that to do so would cost the people of this country a great deal more than it would today. Here is a case where Dr. Durie's definition of pollution to which I have previously referred fits very well. This plant discharges waste into the Ottawa river. It discharges gases into the air which, fortunately for the Ontario side of the river, are generally swept away by the prevailing wind. Even more important, it occupies an area which should be beautified for the nation. Those of us who have any aesthetic sense at all are convinced, I am sure, that this building must be moved out of Hull.
Because I say this, I do not want anyone to consider for a moment that I do not realize the practical difficulties. There are thousands of people in Hull who work at this plant. Their rights must be protected, and they can be protected if this plant is moved a few miles down river and good roads are put in so that they can travel easily to work. They might even find it easier to get to work than they do now; so there need be no real hardship to workers.

the unity of our country, which we are celebrating in this centennial year, cannot be too greatly praised.

Having visited his riding I know his electors are justly proud of their member of parliament. I note that he commented upon the fact that Newfoundland has been a part of Canada for only 18 years. An expert in agriculture, I am sure that he will make a great contribution to the House of Commons especially at a time when agriculture is finally receiving the consideration it deserves from the government. In this connection I think of the many bills passed at the last session and of the results that will be forthcoming from the task force mentioned in the speech from the throne.
I congratulate also all my colleagues in this house who have taken part in this debate and who have done it in such a progessive way.
I join with my hon. friend from Nicolet-Yamaska in congratulating our new Quebec leader, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand). As a Quebecker and a French Canadian I am proud to be associated with him. As a Liberal, I am proud to serve under him. As a Canadian, I am proud of his great contribution to my country.
I must also congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) on his fine speech and I am looking forward to hearing another similar speech from him in the next throne speech debate or, rather, debates.

To the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) may I say that my delight in having heard another of his speeches is, however, tinged by sadness when I think of the centennial project of Mr. Camp.
May 16, 1967



A moment ago I mentioned the Minister of Manpower and Immigration. I join with him when he says:
As a French Canadian, I am celebrating the centennial of confederation because there is something to celebrate.
I am going to talk for a few minutes on some of the achievements of the past and some of my hopes for the future.
The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo mentioned the poverty that faced his riding before Newfoundland joined confederation. This threat of poverty was widespread throughout the then colonies in 1867. We have since built a country whose standard of living is envied by nations around the world. Poverty has been almost entirely wiped out. This is something to celebrate.
Here I want to pause, because I just said that poverty has been almost entirely wiped out. Alas, it still exists in some parts of the country. As long as it does, as long as some of our fellow-citizens live in conditions of deprivation, we cannot take total pride in being Canadians. The fact that the country as a whole is growing richer, the fact that the number of poor is diminishing does not detract from the urgency of the problem. Indeed, it makes it even more urgent. The fact that we have not used our great wealth to abolish poverty in Canada is a disgrace. It is as simple as that.
This government has done much to fight poverty. I am thinking in particular of some of the programs of the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development (Mr. Sauve).
I must congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) for his proposal of a study on the possibility of a guaranteed income for every Canadian. But more remains to be done. We have the capacity. Everybody knows that. Let us use it. The elimination of poverty in Canada must be our first priority and perhaps it should also be our greatest Centennial project.
I turn now to the matter of the constitution. Of course, I am not an expert in such a field, but nevertheless my few years of experience with the constitution allow me to utter a few words about it. One must however admit that the constitution has, over 100 years, served us very well. We have progressed from a small colonial federation to a great independent nation, the senior member of the Commonwealth and a potential founder of "la franco-phonie". Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to enter this historical debate, having spent some months in preparation for such an occasion. However, the length of time occupied by my discourse this evening will not be long.
At the outset I would join with others in congratulating the mover and seconder of the address in reply, the hon. member for Bu-rin-Burgeo (Mr. Jamieson) and the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Cot6). The topics they chose were important ones, and their eloquence measured up to the responsibilities that they accepted.
I should like to discuss some features of the speech from the throne. It does not say much about the financial and monetary policies of the government, and we of the Social Credit party wish that it did say a little more. At the moment, Canada is in a somewhat brightened situation as far as credit and money supply are concerned, but I would warn the house that already the storm signals are out. This morning's Montreal Gazette carried a column headed: "Is the economy moving once more toward monetary restraint?" It seems, Mr. Speaker, that we cannot go very long without a tightening up of the money supply, and we have only to remember the severe tightening that took place during the winter months. The Bank Act was passed and the money supply seemed to ease somewhat. I trust this article means there is not an election in the immediate offing, though I submit that it does mean that there will be one some time in 1968 and that a tightening of the money supply toward the fall and winter of this year will allow for subsequent expansion to coincide with political demands. I am afraid that it will be a long, long time before our monetary policy functions separate and apart from the political demands of the moment.
I was happy to see in the speech from the throne that the government will move to broaden the scope of the area development incentive program. I trust that when these words were written into the speech from the throne one of the broadenings that the government had in mind was to allow for an extension of this program to allow for development in the tourist industry. Coming from the province of British Columbia, Mr. Speaker, where the tourist industry is the second most valuable industry at the present time, I believe the time is long past when it
May 16, 1967	COMMONS
should receive more consideration than it has been receiving from so many federal statutes.
I cite, for example, the Veterans Land Act and the area incentive program, which operate as if the tourist industry had never been heard of or, if it existed at all, was not worthy of either assistance or commendation. We in British Columbia know that this is now a long standing industry, a permanent one, and that it will shortly be the most important industry we have. It is time that this industry was recognized, and I hope that the section of the speech from the throne dealing with this subject is an indication that it will now be recognized.
I am also happy to see that a special study of the needs of urban development is going to be made. I hope that the study will be a rapid one and will be quickly translated into action. Certainly our present legislation dealing with urban redevelopment sorely needs rewriting. As the situation stands now, it is necessary for a section of a city to degenerate into an absolute slum before the machinery which provides federal assistance can swing into action.
At the present time it is probably more in the financial interest of a city to let an area that is degenerating go all the way to ruin than to move on their own, part way along the line, and attempt to rebuild. I trust that when legislation to deal with this subject is brought in it will enable the federal government to step in to prevent the degeneration of urban areas, and allow the hearts and cores of our cities and towns across the country to be reconstructed and rebuilt, as a better alternative to construction of new buildings on the outskirts, as happens at present. I know that the city of Vernon is interested in this proposed study. It hopes that the subsequent legislation will permit its most imaginative program to go ahead. The city of Revelstoke has also done work in urban redevelopment. Any change for the better in this area would be beneficial not only for my constituency, but also for the nation.

May I remind the house of the eloquent speech of the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Jamieson) who spoke of the power of television. We underestimate that power, and when we bring it to this institution we do not know what the effects will be. During the session we hope to legislate with respect to educational television. We move television into the classroom without knowing what we have done to that classroom or to the educational process. We know we have changed the process and changed it vastly.
We shall change this body by televising it, but we shall not necessarily make it a bit more democratic. I suspect that it will be somewhat less democratic, because the purposes of this chamber are debate and legislation, and not entertainment: And entertainment is the prime purpose of television. The throne speech with its inherent weaknesses was televised; its English has been criticized from end to end of the country; yet the one

thing we do know is that the process of televising did not improve it.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
Democracy is a tender plant and is disappearing from many countries of the world. It exists, in the main, in countries that are constitutional monarchies. That is why in Canada's one hundredth year I am glad that we are still a constitutional monarchy-that we have a Queen of Canada. I trust this situation will continue through the next hundred years and longer because although this may seem contradictory, it is one of the guarantees of the democratic process. When we have moved in all the features of modern technology and stripped away all the mystery and all the ritual from our parliamentary system we shall not have made it more democratic; we shall simply have made it duller in the eyes of the public and the public may decide to do without it.
If we waste time in this institution we do not waste it on the day the speech from the throne is delivered or on the days when we go for royal assent. We waste it in this chamber because we cannot amend our rules and procedures so that we may have the ritual, the dignity, the pageantry, the democracy and the legislation at the same time.
Democracy is, as I have said, a tender growth. We cannot be over-confident about its continued existence. We must be prepared to fight for it. It can suffer, as plants do, from too much kindness; it can suffer from overexposure. I suggest that all hon. members as we begin this second century should think carefully about the purpose of this representative institution of parliament, which until now has been our best guarantee of the continuance of the democratic process in a nation. Although we may feel sometimes that by going more directly to the people and by involving them somehow in the day to day activities of this house through television we are making this institution more democratic, I suspect that the opposite would be true. Only if we could televise every speaker in every section of the house every minute of our sittings might we make it more democratic. But we could not afford the bill, and I submit that the general public would not have the time to watch the proceedings.
I have found in my constituents and in others a measure of trust in the democratic process and in the people they send here to represent them. I think we should be happy to see ourselves in the capacities of debaters and legislators. We can be entertainers during

the campaigns or when we go home to our constituencies. Our job here is quite different.

I wish to join others who have spoken in congratulating the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They made very imaginative speeches -perhaps I should emphasize the word "imaginative" because it takes a lively imagination to see a comprehensive legislative program in the speech prepared by the government.
There were a lot of words in it, containing high-sounding sentiments such as the following:
With our forefathers the fight was against the immense odds of nature on our half of this continent. Today the main struggle is against social injustice, against cultural mediocrity, against spiritual stagnation and against all forms of intolerance.
These are high-sounding words, but, as I say, there is little indication of legislation to put them into effect. There are many contradictions in the speech but I wish at this time to draw the attention of the house to two examples only. In the speech the government said it would take special measures in particularly designated areas where human resources are not adequately utilized. In this connection, so the speech says, parliament will be invited to broaden the scope of the area development incentive program.
This would appear to indicate that the government intends to see that all areas of Canada are assisted in reaching their full potent:al. However, further on in the speech we read that parliament will be asked to pass legislation to assist Canadians to move from their homes in certain areas in order to obtain employment in other areas. I fully support the area development incentive program, which can be of great help to the prairies. But I do not wish to see the government concentrating on moving people from certain areas to find work in other areas. I believe it would be much better to help establish industries and manufacturing plants in areas where there is under-employment.
In this regard I wish to refer to the latest press release issued by the Department of Transport-I take this as an example since I believe most of the departments work on similar lines. It refers to contracts issued during the month of April; it contains four pages listing contracts which have been awarded- $22,000, $26,000, $18,000, $76,000 and so on. Contracts are awarded to firms in British

The Address-Mr. Pascoe Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland, the Northwest Territories and the Yukon.
