In the speech from the throne the government proposes changes in the rules of parliament, changes that will limit debate, in other words imposing closure. It is no less than that. The plan of the government is further indicated by the replacing of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mcllraith) as house leader by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen). The latter will also be chairman of the house rules committee. His desire to curtail opposition speeches has been very evident during the past few sessions.
There is a contradiction in the speech from the throne in regard to house procedure. It is stated that the rules and methods of parliamentary government must be revised, but it is also stated that parliament must be provided with every facility to ensure that efficiency and thoroughness of deliberations which, in the consideration of every item of public business, is alone the sure protection of the liberty and well-being of our people.
Members on the government side apparently must have short memories, or perhaps I should say convenient memories. Some of them were not in opposition when the Diefenbaker government was in office and I suggest they should read Hansard of 1957, 1958, 1959, 1960, 1961 and 1962. There are some members on the government side who will remember their opposition tactics. They will remember how they criticized and debated government policies. They will recall the day after day wrangling over estimates of the various government departments, particularly the Department of Agriculture. Perhaps I should put on record some of their remarks as they defended their rights as opposition critics. Their statements appear in earlier issues of Hansards.
The Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh) when in opposition stated on October 4, 1962, as recorded in Hansard at page 227 for that date:
All members of the opposition were elected for one purpose and that was in opposition to the government.
IMr. Pascoe.]
The hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Hai-dasz), when in opposition, as recorded at page 398 of Hansard for October 11, 1962, said:
Since it is the duty of members of the loyal opposition to oppose I cannot see how one can have effective opposition without constructive criticism... before we realize it, Mr. Speaker, political criticism may unfortunately be regarded as an un-Canadian activity instead of democracy's greatest safeguard ... I believe that no reform can be achieved and no survival is possible without the freedom of honest and vigorous criticism.
The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) when he was in opposition had this to say, as recorded at page 349 of Hansard for February 4, 1963:
So, Mr. Speaker, surely it is the duty of all members of the opposition in this house to give the people a chance to return what they would consider to be a better government. We can only do that by getting rid of this one and that can only be done by taking a united stand.
I might point out that in that united stand the Liberal members voted with Social Credit for debt free money.
Here is a small quotation from the March, 1967, issue of Canada Month. I think it is written with tongue in cheek but it indicates the attitude of the government:
On January 18, for the first time since the fall of 1964, the ruling Pearson junta was defeated in a House of Commons vote. It was on an amendment to the transportation bill. The transport minister, J. W. Pickersgill, crystalized the good old Liberal attitude about governing with the classic comment that the defeat "humiliated" him. What makes these opposition fellows think this is a democracy, hmm? Where do they think they get off, voting against a government bill?
Parliament, admittedly, may not be perfect but it is far superior to any form of totalitarian rule or dictatorship. Parliament is not an assembly line process for the mass production of government measures. No democracy such as ours can ever streamline its political machinery to the point of curtailing free parliamentary debate-reasonable debate carried on for one definite purpose. In the nine years that I have been an M.P. I consider that house debates have been directed to the one purpose of improving legislation, or suggesting better legislation.
Opposition members not only help to amend legislation, they also inform Canadians of what is involved and how each measure affects national, provincial and individual interests. Sound legislation will come out of parliament only if there is constructive criticism and the presentation of alternative viewpoints. Despite government charges of delaying the business of parliament, and despite
May 16, 1967	COMMONS
unfriendly press reports I am sure Canadians understand that the role of an opposition member is to criticize government measures and try to improve them. This is democratic government.
The throne speech refers to the appointment of a special task force to propose longterm national agricultural policies. According to a press report the aim is to lift Canada's farm industry to a level comparable to that enjoyed by other segments of the economy. This is an admission that farm income under present government policies is too low.
The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Brand) has submitted an amendment seeking price improvements for the dairy industry. I agree with his arguments in this regard, but I want to make a few references to wheat farming, particularly on the prairies. A brief reference to a recent address by Dr. J. C. Gilson, head of the department of agricultural economics of the University of Manitoba, will put the situation in clear focus:
A truly national farm policy does not exist in Canada at the present time. Nor do we have a clearly definitive idea of what the philosophy and objectives of such a national policy ought to be. What we appear to have is a confusing collection of policies, many of which were created in times of emergency and which have been patched and perpetuated long after the original crises have disappeared.
The suggestions to the government contained in the report of the standing committee on agriculture should, I think, be used by this proposed task force when it meets, and I will deal with them just briefly. They suggest convening a national conference on farm policy under the auspices of the federal government. Perhaps this could start off the work of the proposed farm task force. They also mention the need for the production of a billion bushels of wheat per year in Canada by 1980, in order to meet world demand.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
I suggest the government should not be too complacent about this. The latest D.B.S. review shows that exports from the United States and Australia were higher this year than last and that exports from Canada and the Argentine were lower. This report relates to the August to February period of the current crop year. The graph shows that exports of wheat and wheat flour from Canada were down.
The committee recommends a continuation of the Canadian food aid program, and I think we will all agree that there is a need
DEBATES	303
The Address-Mr. Pascoe for an expansion in this regard. The committee also recommended very definitely that the price of wheat be increased by 50 cents a bushel. The full implications of the recent increase in the price of wheat have not yet become apparent, but the 21 cent per bushel announced is far below the recommended 50 cent increase. The committee also recommended an increase in the initial price for wheat at the delivery point. Surely this is a logical move in view of the recently announced increased price.
It has been said that every effort should be made to ensure that tolls on the St. Lawrence seaway be either eliminated or kept to a minimum and that capital costs should be accepted as far as possible as a direct responsibility of the people of Canada under a national policy. I need not point out that not long ago the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) announced lockage fees for the Welland canal commencing April 1. This charge has been imposed, and I should like to read a few headings from the latest edition of the Ship-Shore news of April this year. These headings are: "Lockage charges will harm Quebec says Trois-Rivieres"; "Fees hinder export, domestic trade says Maple Leaf Mills", and "Flood of protests greets announcement of lock fees".
A telegram from Charles W. Gibbings, president of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, was sent to the Minister of Transport, and I should like to read part of it. It states:
Prairie farmers greatly disturbed at federal government decision to reimpose a toll structure called a lockage fee on the Welland canal which Canada has long considered a domestic waterway and which now will become the only domestic waterway in North America to carry user tolls.
I think that pretty well explains the stand taken by the shippers and the prairie wheat pools regarding these lockage fees.
The committee also said that country elevators must not be considered as places for storage but should have storage facilities connected with them. In this connection let me point out the strategic location of the federal government elevator at Moose Jaw which has a capacity of 5,500,000 bushels. It is located on the main line of the C.P.R. and can also be served by the C.N.R. This elevator has a very important potential use in line with the committee's proposals. A number of members of the agriculture committee toured the southern part of our prairie provinces and visited this elevator. They were quite impressed with its facilities and I should like to urge the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters)
May 16, 1967

The Address-Mr. Pascoe and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) to give close consideration to the potential use of this elevator.
I might say that the elevator at Moose Jaw is nearly full of wheat. It is being used to a capacity of 5,250,000 bushels, with the rest of the space being utilized for wheat cleaning. It is in extremely good condition and can be put to good use, particularly in view of the reference to storage for emergencies. This elevator would be adaptable for that purpose. I intended to make a few other comments in this regard but I shall defer them until I have another opportunity to speak on the supply motion. In conclusion let we refer to an editorial which appeared in the Ottawa Journal on May 10 regarding the extraordinary length of the speech from the throne and the looseness of its composition, which made it not a useful and reliable forecast of legislation but a kind of inventory of the desires and dreams of the government.
Dreams are not to be discouraged but there can be danger in too much dreaming. Government programs must give encouragement to initiative and hard work and there must be room for private enterprise. Care must be taken that Canada does not become a welfare state in which there is a concept that society owes every citizen a living, regardless of his willingness or ability to work. In this regard I draw attention to the front page of the May issue of Canada Month. The featured heading is "Allan J. MacEachen, minister of the workless future". Canadians do not want a workless future, they want an opportunity to earn their own living, and we in the opposition intend to see that these aspirations are fulfilled.
The throne speech has been aptly described as a "scatter gun" approach to pressing problems facing the government. It contains a long list of generalities, with little indication of a positive legislative program. We on this side intend to press for quick action on the agricultural cost-price squeeze and the housing crisis, as well as ever increasing consumer prices.
The government could delay tackling these pressing problems by stirring up early debate on emotional issues such as capital punishment, divorce laws and the national anthem. Vague references in the throne speech to regional, national and international issues make it possible for the government to have this session drag on as long as the last one. If this session is another year-long one, the blame will lie with the government in its priority 
list. Only the government can decide the order of legislation, and it is up to the government to have parliament tackle problems in the order of greatest need. We want this to be fully understood by the public. If there is a delay the fault must rest with the government.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. S. Macdonald (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to commence my remarks on the occasion of this debate with words of congratulation to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. The subject on which I should like to touch might perhaps be headed under the title of the public interest and the individual and I will commence with the recognition that big government is with us to stay.
There is no point in the kind of wishful thinking so often indulged in by members of the financial community, that suddenly in some way the vast apparatus of government will be dismantled. The fact is it will not be, because I believe the majority of people are in support of the benefits and improvements which have been brought about by government intervention. However, because government has become so big and because its operations have extended into so many aspects of our lives, I am concerned with whether it is being fairly administered in the individual case. My concern therefore is as to the quality of administration. Is it humane; does it do equity, and can it adjust itself to the rich variety of individual personality which is represented in our society?
My feeling is that the answer to those three questions is a qualified negative, and I should like to cite a number of examples which indicate to me that our apparatus of government is concerned too much with being efficient and not enough with being humane. I prefer to do so under three headings: First, suggested changes in the criminal law, second, suggested changes in the civil legal system under federal jurisdiction and, third, by suggesting an administrative review procedure.
Having regard to the Criminal Code, my first comment is how old fashioned it is. Basically it dates from 1892, and it in turn was based on the Stephen draft of 1880, which in turn largely codified the accumulated practices of centuries.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
We have had revisions, it is true, but they have been largely housekeeping changes in
May 16, 1967	COMMONS
the nature of tidying up the effect of court decisions and occasionally recognizing technological innovations such as the airplane or that famous card game 3-card monte. I should like to pick out two things to illustrate my point of view. The first is the regime for bail in lieu of custody pending trial and, second, the right to counsel before trial.
With regard to bail, in the Criminal Code it is not mandatory that in every case a person suspected of an offence be arrested and held in custody pending trial. Under the Criminal Code the local authorities are given a discretion to issue a summons to require the accused to appear in answer to the accusation rather than to issue a warrant for his arrest and detention. In a very large number of cases, however, the local authorities insist on using the arrest rather than the summonsing procedure, and therefore a problem arises.
Once an accused is arrested he then must use the bail procedure to regain his liberty pending trial. While the bail procedure is intended to relieve against detention pending trial, in my opinion it is more oppressive than it is relieving. What this means in practice, at least in the metropolitan area from which I come, is that a man, who in law otherwise is presumed innocent until proven guilty, must be able to arrange two things on short notice. First, he must find someone to provide cash or proof of property and, second, he must be able to arrange the attendance of a provincial official, that is a justice of the peace. Failing that-and I can assure you that it fails quite easily late at night or on a holiday-the law treats the accused in the same way he would be treated had he already been convicted of a major offence. He is locked up under maximum security conditions.
I should like to make clear to members of the house that they do not need to rely on my opinion of the way the bail system works. It has been thoroughly documented in the very able study by Professor Martin Friedland of the University of Toronto law school in a book entitled "Detention Before Trial". Before referring to some of his detailed findings I should like to refer to the following at page 172:
The period before trial is too important to be left to guesswork and caprice. At stake in the process is the value of individual liberty. Custody during the period before trial not only affects the mental, social and physical life of the accused and his family, but also may have a substantial impact on the result of the trial itself. The law should abhor any unnecessary deprivation of liberty and positive steps should be taken to ensure that detention before trial is kept to a minimum
DEBATES	305
The Address-Mr. D. S. Macdonald
By way of illustration of the effect of the administration of the Criminal Code in Toronto I should like to read the following summary of the facts in Professor Friedland's study. I am quoting from page 174:
Of those arrested by the police, which is over 90 per cent of those charged, approximately 85 per cent are kept in police custody until their first court appearance, many for substantial periods of time. Most persons arrested during the day are not brought into court that day, even though the court is sitting . .. The study revealed, for example, that in one division station over 80 per cent of all those booked between 7.00 a.m. and midnight were kept in police custody for over 10 hours before their first court appearance. For all of metropolitan Toronto, 84 per cent of all persons arrested for criminal offences were kept in custody until their first court appearance. Approximately 40 per cent of those who appeared in court in custody for their first court appearance, 95 per cent of whom did not have a lawyer, pleaded guilty at that time. A thorough revision of the procedural aspects of release before the first court appearance is clearly necessary.
He goes on to point out that many persons whose cases are not disposed of at the first court appearance spend substantial periods of time in custody pending the disposition of their cases. The use of cash or property bail as the determinant for securing attendance at trial inevitably involves a discrimination between rich and poor in the administration of the criminal law. Let the comparison be made between the treatment accorded someone accused of white collar crime, like Mrs. Viola MacMillan, with that accorded the poor unfortunates disgorged from the Don jail after a week end. I think it is clear that there is different treatment. The goddess of justice in the traditional statue may be blind, but one wonders whether it is cash that she is weighing on the scales.
Let us go back to the fundamentals. What is the purpose of custody pending trial, or bail in lieu thereof? It is to secure the attendance of the accused at trial. But, how often and in what kinds of case, do accused persons flee from bail, or more fundamentally, what probability is there that an accused will flee? I suggest that in a very high percentage of cases there are external non-legal factors which will deter the accused from disappearance such as family, business interests, roots in the community and insufficient means to evade justice. The minister suggests also a sense of honesty. In those limited cases where moments of panic cause the accused to flee, the efficacy of detection will secure the ultimate apprehension of all but a few.
At this point I should like to say just a few words about the hard core of professional
306	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion criminals who appear to be the standard by which some law enforcement officers regard the rest of society. The bail system need hold no terrors for organized crime in cases where the accused can expect to be eligible for bail. Bail money and counsel will be readily available for the professional criminal. I submit that a ready distinction can be drawn between those who are accused of major crimes against person and property, and the vast majority who run afoul of the law for offences such as impaired driving or a similar offence. My recommendation, therefore, is that the provisions of the Criminal Code requiring that an accused person be taken into custody for a broad spectrum of offences should be sharply curtailed and that many offences should be exempted from the necessity of custody and therefore of bail. I should like to spell out the changes I have in mind later.
Perhaps I might call it ten o'clock.
A motion to adjourn the house under provisional standing order 39A deemed to have been moved.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS- CONSULTATION RESPECTING CULTURAL AGREEMENT WITH BELGIUM
DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS- CONSULTATION RESPECTING CULTURAL AGREEMENT WITH BELGIUM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 8 last, here in Ottawa, an agreement was signed by the governments of Canada and the kingdom of Belgium on the fields of culture, education, science and engineering.
Due to the nature of this international agreement, its implementation will affect fields of provincial jurisdiction, and the central government did not consult the provinces or the Quebec government before negotiating such educational and cultural relations.
This new procedure raises some doubts on the constitutional level, antagonizes Quebec, and departs from the procedure followed in the fall of 1965 when a cultural agreement was signed between Ottawa and Paris.
According to the letter and the spirit of section 93 of the Canadian constitution, education comes under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures. Culture must be related to education since it is its direct expression and since the fathers of Canadian confederation in 1867 did not dissociate education from culture in the distribution of government responsibilities.
[Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale)J
DEBATES	May 16. 1967
Furthermore, since the Statute of Westminster, that is since December 11, 1931, section 132 of our constitution became dead letter, and the central government can take its stand on no other section to assume the exclusive power to act in international relations, especially in matters exclusively provincial, as education, culture and natural resources.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
The argument is sound: if Ottawa does not have the right of implementation in a given matter, it could not have the exclusive right of negotiation. Indeed, it was in that spirit that, in 1948, Canada subscribed to United Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights, making known some reservations about provincial responsibilities in such matters.
In the 11 articles of the recent Canada-Belgium agreement, Ottawa included no such reservation; it did not have previous consultations with the provinces in general and with Quebec in particular and did not officially provide for the role of the provinces and of Quebec on the permanent joint commission created by that agreement.
Hon. Daniel Johnson, premier of Quebec, and some of his colleagues were entirely right when they protested against the offhand, autocratic and centralizing way in which this Liberal federal government again proceeded in this matter.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that if the Pearson government had decided to humiliate Quebec in its authority and its responsibilities, if it were trying by all direct and indirect means to weaken the provincial fields of jurisdiction, it would have acted exactly as it did in the negotiations about the signing of that agreement between Canada and Belgium.
In the interest of Canada, I hope that the stubbornness of the present central government will stop and that at the meeting of the prime ministers, next July 5, a clear and definite understanding will be reached.
In the field of international jurisdiction, I wish to make a few suggestions about the responsibilities which are exclusively provincial. In fact, I once said:
As far as I am concerned, I feel that the Quebec government can negotiate international treaties without the approval of the central government. But, in order to strike a proper medium in the implementation of true federalism and to enable Canada to put up a peaceful front before foreign countries, I would suggest that the Quebec government inform Ottawa of its initiatives so that Canadian policies do not appear incongruous and incoherent abroad.
May 16. 1967

In the field of shared responsibilities which are mentioned in section 95 of the constitution such as agriculture and immigration, the Quebec government should discuss these matters with Ottawa and come to an agreement beforehand concerning the division of responsibilities.
Finally, where responsibilities lie exclusively with the federal government, Quebec should submit its request to Ottawa and the matter should be decided jointly with the province.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. S. Macdonald (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS- CONSULTATION RESPECTING CULTURAL AGREEMENT WITH BELGIUM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not accept the arguments of the hon. member, for I suggest that he, is confusing the negotiation of treaties, which is the exclusive right of the federal government and always has been, with the implementation of treaties which, depending on the subject matter, may be within provincial competence.
It has long been the practice of Canadian governments to consult the provinces before undertaking any commitment on their behalf, by entering into an international agreement which would require provincial legislation or other provincial action in order to be implemented. I can assure the house that there has been no departure from this practice in the case of the Belgian agreement. In signing a cultural agreement with Belgium the Canadian government has naturally committed only itself and federal agencies concerned with cultural matters. This was our constitutional right.
So far as the provinces are concerned, the agreement only provides a framework which could facilitate the participation of provincial authorities which might be interested in cultural exchanges with Belgium. The agreement clearly does not commit any province to do anything in connection with cultural exchanges with Belgium unless it wishes to develop such exchanges, in which case ample opportunity has been provided for full consultation. Thus the agreement will make it possible for Canadian efforts to strengthen our relations with Belgium through cultural exchanges at the federal and provincial level to be co-ordinated in a manner consistent with our constitutional requirements, and with the unity of purpose which must characterize our action in the international field.
The Prime Minister wrote each premier on May 3 to make it clear that there will be full consultation with the provinces as to any course of action they might wish to take in any matter arising out of this agreement which would involve provincial jurisdiction or require provincial implementation.
DEBATES	307
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
With respect to the right of the Canadian government to negotiate and conclude such agreements, both the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs have, on numerous occasions in the house, stated the constitutional position in Canada which clearly gives the federal government exclusive responsibility for the conduct of our country's external affairs and for the negotiation and conclusion of agreements with foreign governments in all fields.

maintopic: WATER RESOURCES-REPORTED AGREEMENT TO ESTABLISH NATIONAL ADVISORY COUNCIL ON POLLUTION
WATER RESOURCES-REPORTED AGREEMENT TO ESTABLISH NATIONAL ADVISORY COUNCIL ON POLLUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over a period of five years I have placed the following resolution on the order paper:
That, in the opinion oi this house, the government should consider the advisability of the creation of a water pollution control division, composed of representatives of the ten provinces, within the framework of the proposed national resources council, with powers and funds required to institute research programs, collect, collate and analyse water control data, and to co-ordinate the water pollution control objectives for the provinces; in addition, to further the study of water pollution control problems of a national character.
Then, Mr. Speaker, I was very interested to read in the Vancouver Sun of May 6 a statement made by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Pepin). The heading of the article is "Ministers Agree on Pollution Group; National Council Offered as Solution to Problem". The article reads:
Federal and provincial resource ministers and government officials agreed in principle Friday to set up a national advisory council on water pollution.
It will set goals and co-ordinate the work of various government agencies in Ottawa and the provinces, Energy Minister Jean Luc Pepin told a press conference.
With representation from the two senior levels of government and probably some universities, the body will have a secretariat provided by the federal government.
Pepin said his proposal was received favourably but no firm decision could be made at a two-day round of meetings of resource ministers because some provinces wanted to clear the decision with their cabinets.
In making that statement, the minister no doubt accepted in principle the resolution I had been moving in the house for five years. In that connection, I was very interested to read in the Toronto Daily Star of Monday, May 15, an article written by Walter Gray, who is very interested in the conservation of
May 16, 1967

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion natural resources, entitled, "Will water pollution control sink in sea of provincialism?" The article reads, in part:
Little wonder that W. H. Herridge (N.D.P.- Kootenay West), one of the most outspoken conservationists on parliament hill-
I have to read this, although I do not like this sort of thing because I am so modest at heart.
-got up In the Commons the other day and cried plagiarism against the government.
For the last 15 years he has made an annual plea for the establishment of a national advisory council on water pollution, but every time his private bill was sunk without a trace.
Then, to his surprise, he received a press release from the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, announcing that resources minister Jean Luc Pepin had proposed to the provinces the establishment of just such a council.
Pepin, of course, did not credit Herridge with the idea: rather, he said it came from last fall's national pollution conference in Montreal, sponsored by the Canadian Council of Resource Ministers.
I asked my question as a result of a number of people on this side of the house saying to me: well, the government has actually adopted a policy you have advocated for some years. It was for that reason, Mr. Speaker, I asked this question of the minister:
I wish to address a question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources which is of urgent and prime national importance. Is it correct that the federal government has accepted in principle a resolution that has been placed on the order paper for over five years by the hon. member for Kootenay West, by an agreement in principle between the federal and provincial resource ministers to establish a national advisory council on water pollution? Can the minister inform the house of any such proposal or agreement?
However, Mr. Speaker, once again you nipped me in the bud when you rose and said:
Order, please. I do not think the question and the hon. member's assertions are acceptable at this time.
As a matter of fact, I was a bit nettled by that. It was for that reason I suggested I would have an opportunity of dealing with the question a little more fully after ten o'clock, as I am doing now. I hope when the parliamentary secretary replies to my proposal he will at least give some credit to the members of this group for advancing a constructive suggestion to the government over a number of years. I must say also I was not very pleased that the government acted along

the lines it did when making the minister's announcement.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Davis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
maintopic: WATER RESOURCES-REPORTED AGREEMENT TO ESTABLISH NATIONAL ADVISORY COUNCIL ON POLLUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Kootenay West raises a very important subject, the pollution of water. He also makes what under other circumstances might be a very serious charge; that is, the charge of plagiarism.
His proposals of recent years have had to do with the setting up of a national board or council, with powers and certain administrative capabilities, as I understand it. This is not what is envisaged. This is not the subject which has been discussed by the Canadian council of resource ministers. Instead, what has been discussed is a purely advisory council, which perhaps would set up standards on an agreed basis which would be embodied in legislation, both federally and provincially, across the country. The council will advise as to areas of profitable research and as to successful methods of dealing with pollution. In other words, it would be an advisory body, not one with powers.
The hon. member made some reference to consistency. A few days ago his party moved a motion in this house to the effect that the government of the day-the present government-had not seen fit to give special status to one of our provinces, notably Quebec. I suggest that this was a recognition of the powers of the provinces, a la mode, so to speak. We have a division of powers as between provinces and the national government of this country. The advisory council, I submit, does recognize the fact that there is an area of divided jurisdiction in respect to pollution, and this can be covered adequately only by consultation at the federal-provincial level.
There was a meeting recently of the Canadian Council of Resource Ministers, and at that meeting the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources put forward the idea that an advisory committee be set up. This matter was discussed and the idea was received favourably by some representatives of provincial governments; others wished to consider the matter at some length. There were three main headings under which the council could study this matter. The council would study the possibility of setting up
May 16. 1967

agreed lists of objectives and standards Second, it would conduct research into causes and ways of reducing pollution, federal and provincial. Third, it would advise the governments, federally and provincially, on water pollution problems and programs for their solution.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion In other words, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has proposed that an advisory council be set up. This is under consideration, and the establishment of this council will be discussed again when the m.nisters meet this fall.
